children.text: ) yata evam "iti" tasmāt "nānavasthā" prāguktā | atha sahakāriṇā kṣityādinā kuśūlādyavastho 'pi bījādiḥ tenāpi kṣityādiḥ kṛtaviśeṣa evopatiṣṭhetānavasthaivaṃ syāt iti | tasya prakārasyānabhyupagamāt puruṣaprayatnādereva kṣetraprakiraṇahetoravyavahitasnigdhapṛthivībījasamparkalakṣaṇasya kāryotpādānuguṇaviśeṣajanakasya viśeṣe 'syopagamāt | tatra yaduktaṃ pareṇa ‘yathā prathamasamprarkabhājaḥ kṣitibījādayaḥ parasparasya viśeṣamanādadhānāḥ kāryotpādānuguṇaṃ viśeṣaṃ janayanti, tathā sthirarūpā api bhāvāḥ tadekakāryapratiniyatāḥ parasparakṛtaviśeṣanirapekṣā eva bhaviṣyanti'; iti, tadabhyupagacchannāh "tathā yadyakṣaṇiko 'pi" ityādi | kṣaṇikavadakṣaniko 'pi yadi kāryaṃ karoti karotu nāma | nā kaścid vārayati | kintu yena svabhāvena kāryaṃ karoti sa yadi "avilambitakāryakartṛdharmā" akṣepeṇa karotītyevaṃśīlo dharmo yasya sa tathoktaḥ, tadā "pṛthagbhāvasya sambhāvāt kevalo 'pi" na kevalaṃ sahitaḥ "tathā syāt" tatkāryakārakaḥ syādityuktaṃ bahuśaḥ | "atatsvabhāvastu" akṣepakartṛsvabhāvavikalastu "tadāpi" sahitāvasthāyāmapi prāgvat "akāraka eva" pararūpeṇa kartṛtvasya pūrvameva niṣedhāt |
children.translated_text: Since this is so, "therefore" the infinite regress (<s>anavasthā</s>) mentioned earlier [does not arise]. Now, if by the cooperative condition such as earth, even a seed in a granary and the like [is affected], and by that [seed], the earth and so forth would also stand as already specialized — then the infinite regress would indeed follow. [The reply is:] because that mode is not accepted; since human effort (<s>puruṣaprayatna</s>) and the like, which is the cause of scattering in the field, is accepted as the generator of the specialization, having the characteristic of unobstructed contact between moist earth and seed — [that is what generates] the specialization conducive to the production of the effect. Now, regarding what the opponent has said: 'Just as earth, seed, and the like, sharing the first contact, generate a specialization conducive to the production of the effect without conferring specialization on each other, so too entities with stable forms, determined for a single effect, will be independent of specialization produced by each other' — accepting this, he says "Similarly, even if a non-momentary [entity]" and so forth. Even if a non-momentary entity, like a momentary one, produces an effect — let it produce! No one prevents it. However, if the nature by which it produces the effect is "one whose property is to produce the effect without delay" — that is, one whose nature is to act by projection — then, "because of the possibility of separate existence, even alone" — not only when combined — "it would be so," that is, it would be a producer of that effect — this has been stated many times. "But one that does not have that nature" — one that lacks the nature of an agent that acts by projection — "even then," even in the state of being combined, "is a non-agent just as before," because agency in the form of another has already been refuted.

body.translated_text: From what basis, then, is this freedom obtained — that cooperative conditions (<s>sahakārin</s>), producing a sprout and other effects (<s>kārya</s>), generate a series of successive specializations (<s>viśeṣaparamparā</s>) conducive to each other's production of the effect, while a specialization conducive to the production of the effect [arises] merely through proximity in a location free from obstruction and the like? To this he says: "And because of the twofold nature of effects (<s>kārya</s>), it is thus classified." How is there a twofold nature of effects? To this he says: the specializations (<s>viśeṣa</s>) that are generated by the cooperative conditions (<s>sahakārin</s>) in an immediately adjacent location free from obstruction, characterized by a distinct momentary existence relative to each other's prior states — one type of effect is that whose nature involves origination through a succession of these [specializations], in the form of successively more and more particularized momentary existences. And the other, contrary to that, is that which arises merely through the proximity of the cooperative conditions and does not depend on a series of specializations produced by each other. The example here is "like a sprout and so forth"; by the word 'and so forth,' like cooked rice and the like. Likewise, a sense faculty (<s>indriya</s>) whose nature is to act by projection, like its cognition (<s>vijñāna</s>) and so forth. And this qualification is for the purpose of excluding a sense faculty that has entered a covering away from the luminous [source]. How is this known? If asked thus: because of the difference in the intrinsic nature (<s>svabhāva</s>) of effects and causes,

body.text: tadevamekārthakriyayā viśeṣotpādanena cākṣaṇikānāṃ sahakāritvaṃ niṣidhyopasaṃharannāha- "tasmāt" ityādi | dvividhasyāpi sahakāritvasyāyogānnaivākṣaṇikasya kaścit sahakārīti kevalo 'pi svakāryaṃ kuryāditi sahakāripratyayāpekṣasyākṣaṇikasya hetutāṃ bruvāṇasya kiṃ yuktamiti darśayannāha- "prāyastu" ityādi | yo hi sthirahetuvādī tasya yadi sa hetuḥ pratyayāntarāṇyapekṣya kāryaṃ karoti tadā "vyaktam" avaśyaṃ tasya sthirasya hetoḥ pratyayāntarāpekṣakārakasya svabhāvāntarasyotpattiriti | "nākāryasya" kāryatāmananubhavato apekṣetyucyate | yataḥ sahakāriṇāṃ yaḥ "saṃghātaḥ" sannipātaḥ "tatsthāyī" tatra vartamāno bhāvasantānaḥ "prāyaḥ" bāhulyena "sahakāripratyayairupajanitaviśeṣaḥ" san "svakāryaṃ kurvan dṛṣṭo bījādivat" (

children.translated_text: Hbṭ 138

children.text: ) tasmādevaṃ vibhajyate | prāyograhaṇaṃ cākṣepakārīndriyādisaṅghātavyavacchedārtham | tatsambhavino nyāyasyākṣaṇikeṣu pṛthagbhāvasambhavena kathañcidapi kalpayitumaśakyatvāt | prāgakārakasya paścāt kārakasvabhāvāntarotpattistu na virudhyate | tasyaiva hyakārakasya tadātmā kārakaḥ svabhāvo na yujyate na tvatadātmā | ata eva svabhāvāntaragrahaṇam | tatra kevalamakārakasvabhāvasya svarasanirodhitāmātramupeyam | tataḥ sarvaṃ susthamiti |
children.translated_text: Therefore it is thus classified. And the qualification "for the most part" is for the purpose of excluding the assemblage of sense faculties and the like that act by projection. Because the principle that applies to those [projective agents] cannot be devised in any way for non-momentary entities, due to the possibility of separate existence. However, the arising of a different intrinsic nature — agency — in what was previously a non-agent is not contradicted. For it is the nature of agency belonging to that same non-agent that is untenable — not a nature that is not identical with it. For this very reason, the expression "a different intrinsic nature" is used. In that case, one should accept merely the spontaneous cessation of the non-agent nature. Then everything is well-established.

body.translated_text: Having thus refuted the cooperative-condition status of non-momentary entities through both the single purposive action and the production of specialization, he concludes by saying "Therefore" and so forth. Since both types of cooperative-condition status are untenable, no non-momentary entity has any cooperative condition at all, so it would produce its own effect even alone — showing that it is unreasonable for one who asserts the causality of a non-momentary entity that depends on the condition of cooperative factors, he says "For the most part" and so forth. For one who advocates permanent causes (<s>sthirahetuvādin</s>), if that cause produces an effect depending on other conditions (<s>pratyayāntara</s>), then "clearly" — necessarily — an intrinsically different nature must arise in that permanent cause, which produces [the effect] depending on other conditions. "It is not said that a non-effect" — one that does not experience the state of being an effect — "depends [on conditions]." Because the continuum of entities "abiding in that" assemblage (<s>saṃghāta</s>) of the cooperative conditions, "for the most part," having been "endowed with specialization produced by the cooperative conditions," "is seen producing its own effect, like a seed and the like."

body.text: atha matam- kārakasvabhāvāntarotpattiriṣyeta yadi sthirasya hetoḥ prāgapi kārakasvabhāvo na syat | tasya tu prāgapi bhāvāt pratyayāntarāpekṣā tadutpattirapyayukteti ata āha- "kārakasya" ityādi | yadi hi samagrāvasthāyāḥ prāgapi kārakasvabhāvo bhavet tadāsyākriyā na yujyate, saṃhatāvasthāyāmapi tatsvabhvatayaiva karaṇāt, pararūpeṇa kartṛtvasya prāgeva niṣiddhatvāt | na ca karoti | tasmāt so 'sya svabhāvaḥ prāṅnaivāsīt | yadi ca pratyayāntarairapyasau na kriyeta tat kimiti mudhaiva tānyapekṣate? iti |
body.translated_text: Now, if it is thought: the arising of a different intrinsic nature of agency would be accepted only if the permanent cause did not have the nature of agency even before. But since it exists even before, the dependence on other conditions and the arising of that [agency] are also untenable — to this he says "Of the agent" and so forth. For if the nature of agency existed even before the state of being assembled, then its inaction would be untenable, since it would act in the assembled state precisely by virtue of that same nature, and agency in the form of another has already been refuted. Yet it does not act [before assembly]. Therefore that nature simply did not exist in it before. And if it is not produced even by other conditions, then why does it depend on them uselessly?

body.text: 43. nirhetukavināśacarcāyā upasaṃhāraḥ |
body.translated_text: 43. Conclusion of the discussion on destruction without cause.

body.text: tadevaṃ ‘tatsvabhāvasya jananāt'; tyasya ‘yo yatsvabhāvaḥ sa svahetorevotpadyamānaḥ tādṛśo bhavati punastadbhāve hetvantaramapekṣate'; ityasyānekāntaparihārāyoktasya prakārāntareṇānekānte udbhāvite tatparijihīrṣayā "aparāparapratyayayogena" ityādyabhihitam | tatra yena nyāyena kṣaṇikānāṃ hetuphalasvabhāvaḥ tasyākṣaṇikeṣvasambhavaṃ pratipādayituṃ prāsaṅgikaṃ yadupakrāntaṃ tat parisamāpayya prakṛtamanubadhnannāha- "tasmād yo yadātmā" ityādi | yadi svabhāvenāsthitidharmaṇo bhāvasya na nāśakāraṇaiḥ prayojanaṃ svabhāvena sthitidharmaṇo bhaviṣyatītyata āha- "sthitidharmaṇo 'pi" ityādi | sthitidharmaṇo 'pi hi naiva nāśakāraṇaiḥ kiñcit prayojanam | tasya svahetubhyaḥ samupajāto yaḥ sthiraḥ svabhavaḥ tadanyathātvasyāsthirātmatāpatteḥ (

children.translated_text: Hbṭ 139

children.text: ) kenacit kartumaśakyatvāt | kāmaṃ hi bhāvāḥ svayaṃ na bhaveyuḥ | na tu santa eva svaṃ svabhāvaṃ parityajanti | atha sthitidharmaṇo 'pyanyathātvapratipattiriṣyate tadānyathātvapratipattau vā "tatsvabhāva eva" sthitidharmaiva "na syāt" ātmabhūtasyāsthitidharmaṇaḥ svabhāvasya paścāt sambhave prāgapyabhāvāyogāt | nahi tadātmanastasmiṃ(smin) sannihite kadācidabhāvo yuktaḥ, atastvabhāvatāprasaṅgāt ‘viruddhadharmādhyāasya bhedalakṣaṇatvāt'; ityuktam | tathā ca sati "pūrva" eva "vikalpaḥ" svabhāvenāsthitidharmā bhāva iti | "tatra ca" pūrvavikalpe prāgevoktaṃ dūṣaṇaṃ vināśahetorvaiyarthyamiti |
children.translated_text: Entities may indeed not come into being of their own accord. But once existent, they do not abandon their own intrinsic nature. Now, if it is accepted that even one whose nature is permanence undergoes alteration, then either upon accepting that alteration, "it would not be of that very nature" — it would not be of a permanent nature — because if a nature that is intrinsically impermanent could occur later, there is no reason for its absence earlier as well. For it is not tenable that what is of that very nature should at any time be absent when that [entity] is present, because that would entail the absurdity of non-existence; as it has been said, 'because the distinguishing mark of difference is the superimposition of contradictory properties.' That being so, "the first alternative" [stands] — that entities are by nature impermanent. "And in that case," in the first alternative, the previously stated objection applies — namely, the purposelessness of a cause of destruction.

body.translated_text: Thus, with regard to [the statement] 'because of the production of that nature' — that is, [the principle that] 'whatever has such-and-such a nature arises as such only from its own cause and does not require another cause for its recurrence' — which was stated for the removal of the indeterminate reason (<s>anekānta</s>), when the indeterminate reason is raised in another way, in order to remove it, "through the connection with successive conditions (<s>aparāparapratyaya</s>)" and so forth was stated. There, having concluded the digression undertaken to demonstrate that the nature of cause and effect (<s>hetuphala</s>) that applies to momentary entities is impossible for non-momentary ones, he reconnects with the main topic by saying "Therefore, whatever has whatever nature" and so forth. If an entity whose nature is non-permanence has no need for causes of destruction, then what about one whose nature is permanence? To this he says "Even for one whose nature is permanence (<s>sthitidharman</s>)" and so forth. For even for one whose nature is permanence, causes of destruction serve absolutely no purpose, since the stable nature (<s>svabhāva</s>) that has arisen from its own causes cannot be made otherwise by anything, because that would entail the absurdity of its stable nature becoming unstable.

body.text: athāsau śirasvabhāva eva, kevalamasyāśirasvabhāvatā prāgasati vināśahetorupajāyate, anyathā nivṛttyayogādityata āha- "yaśca parasmāt" nāśahetoḥ sthitidharmaṇaḥ sata "anyathābhāvaḥ" asthitidharmatālakṣaṇo bhavati, sa pūrvakāt sthitidharmaṇaḥ svahetusamudbhūtāt svabhāvāt "aparaḥ" anyaḥ "svabhāvastasminniṣpanne" paścā[jjanya]tvād bhinnahetukatvācca "kathaṃ tasya" svabhāvaḥ "syāt"? | tadātmatayā pratibhasanāditi cet | sārūpyādalakṣitavivekasya tathā pratibhāsanaṃ syāt yadyasau pūrvasvabhāve satyevānyato bhavet | anyathā virodhaḥ kathaṃ parihriyeta? | bhavatvaparaḥ svabhāva iti cet | yaścāparaḥ svabhāvaḥ sa kathaṃ tasya? | na hyanyo 'nyasya svabhāvo yuktaḥ, atiprasaṅgāt | yo 'paraḥ svabhāvaḥ sa kimiti tasya na bhavati? ityata āha- "svabhāvabheda-" ityādi | bhavatu vastvantarameva tadaparasvabhāvatayā ko doṣaḥ? ityata āha- "tathā ca" vastvantaratve sati vināśahetorupajāyamānasya svabhāvasya pūrvako bhāvaḥ svahetubhyo yaḥ sthitidharmā jātaḥ so 'cyutidharme sthito nivṛttibhāṅna bhavati, vināśahetorvastvantarotpattau vyāpṛtatvāditi na "tasya" sthitidharmaṇo "'nyathābhāvo" nivṛttiḥ | nahi mugdarādervastvantarasya bhāve 'parasya nivṛttiryuktā, atiprasaṅgāt | tadupamarddena tadutpattau ca prāgeva proktam |
body.translated_text: Now, if [one says] it is indeed of an impermanent nature, but its impermanent nature arises only when the cause of destruction, previously absent, comes into being — otherwise cessation would be impossible — to this he says: "And the alteration" of a permanent, existent entity "arising from another" — namely, a cause of destruction — characterized by the nature of impermanence, is "other" — different — "from the former" nature arisen from the permanent entity's own causes. "When that is accomplished" — since it is produced later and has a different cause — "how could it be the nature of that" [original entity]? If objected that it appears as identical with it — the appearance as such would be possible for one whose distinctness is unnoticed due to similarity, only if that [new nature] arose from something else while the former nature still existed. Otherwise, how would the contradiction be resolved? If it is said, let it be a different nature — then how is that different nature "of that" [entity]? For it is not tenable that one thing is the intrinsic nature of another, due to overextension (<s>atiprasaṅga</s>). Why does the other nature not belong to that [entity]? To this he says "Difference of nature" and so forth. Let it be an altogether different entity — what fault is there in that being a different nature? To this he says: "And in that case," when it is a different entity, the nature arising from the cause of destruction — the entity that was formerly produced from its own causes as having a permanent nature — that [original entity] stands established in a nature free from decay; it does not undergo cessation. Because the cause of destruction is engaged in producing a different entity. Therefore there is no "alteration" — no cessation — "of that" permanent entity. For it is not tenable that the cessation of one thing follows from the existence of another different entity, like a club and the like, due to overextension. And the [possibility of] destruction through impact and production through that [impact] has already been discussed.

body.text: nanu ca dṛśyata eva kaṭhinādirūpasya tāmrāderagnayādervināśahetordravādisvabhāvāntarotpattiḥ | na ca pūrvakasya pracyutidharmatā ityata āha- "etena" anantaroktena "kaṭhinādīnām" ādiśabdād dravādīnāṃ tāmrasuvarṇādināmagniśītavātādibhyo dravatvakaṭhinatvādisvabhāvāntarotpattirvyavasthitarūpasya tāmrādeḥ "pratyuktā" pratyākhyātāḥ, tulyadūṣaṇatvāt |
body.translated_text: But surely it is observed that hard substances such as copper, when acted upon by fire and other causes of destruction, undergo the arising of a different nature such as fluidity, without the former [substance] undergoing decay — to this he says: "By this" — by what was just stated — the arising of different natures such as fluidity and hardness in "hard substances and the like" — by the word 'and so forth,' [including] fluid substances and the like, such as copper and gold, from fire, cold, wind, and the like — "is answered," that is, refuted, because the same objections apply.

body.text: kathaṃ tarhi svabhāvāntarotpattiḥ pūrvasya cāpracyutidharme sthitasyābhāvo yuktaḥ? ityāha- "tatrāpi" kaṭhinādirūpe tāmrādau "pūrvakasya" kaṭhinadravādirūpasya "svarasanirodhitvāt" vināśahetvayogena | "vināśe" sati "agnyādeḥ" ādigrahaṇājjalaniṣekaśītavātādeḥ | sahakāriṇaḥ parasparopasarpaṇādyāśraya pratyayaviśeṣopajātātiśayā "dupādānācca" yat tat kaṭhinādirūpaṃ tāmrādi svarasato nirudhyate | tata eva upādānakāraṇādagnyādisahakārikāraṇopādānapratyayopajātaviśeṣād "apara eva" anya eva dravakaṭhinādisvabhāvo dravagrahaṇasyopalakṣaṇatvāt, "utpanno" na tu pūrvakameva kaṭhinadravādirūpaṃ tāmrādi vyavasthitātmakaṃ dravakaṭhinādisvabhāvena pariṇatamiti |
body.translated_text: How then is the arising of a different essential nature and the cessation of the prior [entity] that persists with the property of non-departure justified? To this he says: "In that case too" — in the form of hardness etc. in copper and so forth — "of the previous one" — having the form of hardness, fluidity, etc. — "because of being self-destructible" — due to the absence of a cause of destruction. "When destruction" occurs, "of fire and so forth" — by the word 'and so forth,' water-sprinkling, cold wind, etc. [are included]. The auxiliary cause, through a special condition based on mutual proximity and the like, having acquired an excellence, "and from the material cause" — that which is copper etc. in the form of hardness etc. is destroyed by its own nature. From that very material cause, with a special excellence acquired from the auxiliary cause such as fire etc. and the material-cause condition, "an entirely different one" — an altogether different essential nature of fluidity, hardness, etc. — the word 'fluidity' being illustrative — "has arisen," but it is not the case that the very same copper etc. having the form of hardness, fluidity, etc., being of a stable nature, has transformed into the essential nature of fluidity, hardness, etc.

body.text: atra para āha- "kenoktaṃ" yathā ‘sthitidharmaṇaḥ sato vināśahetorasthitisvabhāvotpattistato vināśaḥ'; iti, yena ‘yaśca parasmādanyathābhāvaḥ so 'paraḥ svabhāvaḥ'; ityādyucyate | kintu sa svayaṃ sthitidharmaiva svahetubhirjanito nāsyāsthirasvabhāvatā vināśahetorupajāyate | kathaṃ jñāyate yathā ‘svahetubhiḥ svabhāvena sthitidharmaiva janitaḥ'; iti? | vināśahetoragnyāderasambhave avasthānāt | yadi svabhāvenāsthitidharmā svahetorjātaḥ syāt tadā tadasambhave 'pi nāvatiṣṭheta | tasya svabhāvena sthitidharmaṇaḥ svahetubhirevāyamaparaḥ svabhāvo niyamito yaduta "parasmāt" virodhino 'gnyāde "rvināśaḥ svayaṃ bhavatīti" | parasmāditi karmaṇi lyaplope pañcamī paramapekṣya ityarthaḥ | svahetubhirevāyaṃ niyamitasvabhāvo (

children.text: ) jāto yathā tvayā virodhinamapekṣya svayaṃ nirva(va)rtitavyamiti | taduktam-
children.translated_text: ) as: 'you must bring about [destruction] yourself in dependence on the opposing [factor].' Thus it has been said —

body.translated_text: Here the opponent says: "Who has said" that 'from a thing possessing the property of persistence, a non-persistent essential nature arises from the cause of destruction, and from that comes destruction'? — such that one would say 'that which is a change of state from another is a different essential nature' and so on. Rather, it itself, produced by its own causes, is of the very nature of persistence; its unstable essential nature does not arise from the cause of destruction. How is it known that 'it is produced by its own causes as having precisely the property of persistence by its essential nature'? Because it persists when the cause of destruction such as fire etc. is absent. If it had arisen from its own cause as being by nature without the property of persistence, then even in the absence of that [destructive cause] it would not persist. For this [entity] that has the property of persistence by its essential nature, this other nature is determined by its own causes alone, namely: "destruction occurs by itself" "from the opposing" [factor] such as fire etc. 'From the opposing' — the fifth case ending is in the objective sense after dropping the absolutive suffix, meaning 'in dependence on the opposing [factor].' It is born with its essential nature determined by its own causes alone (

body.text:
"svabhāvo 'pi sa tasyetthaṃ yenāpekṣya nivartate |
virodhinaṃ yathānyeṣāṃ pravāho mugdarādikam ||" iti |
body.translated_text: "That essential nature of it is such that, in dependence on which, it ceases — the opposing [factor] — just as for others, the stream [ceases in dependence on] a hammer and the like."

body.text: nanu yadyasya vināśao virodhisannidhāne svayameva bhavatyahetukaḥ prāpnoti, ahetośca deśakālasvabhāvaniyamo na yukta ityata āha- "na ca" naiva vināśo nāma vinaṣṭuraparaḥ svabhāvaḥ, yato 'yaṃ doṣaḥ syāt, kintu "bhāvacyutireva vināśaḥ" | tasyāśca niḥsvabhāvatvāddhetumattā naiva yujyate | nahi sā tasya bhavati | kevalamasau svayameva na bhavati | tato bhaviturabhāvāt kasya hetumattopagamyate? |
body.translated_text: Now, if its destruction occurs by itself in the presence of an opposing [factor], then it would follow that [destruction] is without a cause, and for something without a cause, restriction to [particular] place, time, and nature is not justified. Therefore he says: "And not" — destruction is not at all another entity called 'destroyed,' such that this fault would arise; rather, "the cessation of the entity itself is destruction." And since that [cessation] is without essential nature, being caused is simply not justified. For it does not belong to it [as a positive entity]. It simply does not come into being by itself. Therefore, since what would come into being is absent, whose being-caused is to be accepted?

body.text: siddhāntavādyāha- "nedamanantaroktaṃ vikalpadvayamatikrāmati" | kīdṛśaṃ vikalpadvayam? | ‘kiṃ nityo bhāvaḥ?'; ityādi | nanu ca kālāntarasthitiradharmatāmupagacchato naiva nityavikalpasyāvakāśaḥ | na | tadupagame 'pi nityataivopagatā bhavati | tathā hi- yadyayaṃ saṃvatsarasthitidharmā svahetubhirjanitastadā saṃvatsaraparisamāptau yo 'syādāvudayakāle saṃvatsarasthitidharmā svabhāvo yato 'yaṃ saṃvatsaraṃ sthitaḥ sa eva tadante 'pi | tato 'paraṃ saṃvatsaramavatiṣṭheta | tadante 'pi prathamotpannasaṃvatsarasthitidharmasvabhāvāparityāgādaparāparasaṃvatsarasthitiprasaṅgāt kālāntarasthitidharmatopagame 'pi nityataivopagatā bhavatīti nityavikalpo durnivāraḥ | vināśahetusannidhau svayaṃ nivartata iti copagamādanityavikalpo naśvarātmatāvikalpaḥ | tathā hi- vināśahetvabhimatasannidhau svayaṃ vinaśyato yo 'sya svabhāvaḥ sa eva bhāvasyaikarūpatvādutpannamātrasyeti tadaiva vināśaprasaṅgāt kathamasya kālantarasthitidharmatā sambhavati? | evaṃ vikalpe kṛte pāścātyavikalpopagame kālāntarasthitirevāsya truṭyatīti nityavikalpa evānenopagantavyaḥ | tatra vināśahetusannidhau svayaṃ nāśopagame prāṅnityo bhūtvā paścādanityo vinaśvarasvabhāvo bhavatīti brūte | "evaṃ ca brūvāṇo bhāvadvayaṃ cāha" | vakṣyamāṇāpekṣaścakāraḥ | (

children.text: ) kīdṛśaṃ bhāvadvayam? | nityānityau svabhāvau bhedau yasya tathā | yo 'sau nityaḥ svabhāvaḥ prāktanaḥ tasya nityābhimatasya svayaṃ paścānnāśaṃ brūvāṇaḥ sarvadā pratikṣaṇameva nāśaṃ prāha | anyathā pūrvoktena nyāyena paścādapi nāśāsambhavāt | atha pratikṣaṇamasya nāśo na bhavati tadā paścādapi tadayogāt sarvadaivānāśaṃ prāheti kṛtvā pūrvasminnityābhimate svabhāve vināśaheturasamartho 'kiñcitkara eva |
children.translated_text: ) What kind of duality of entities? That which has two essential natures — eternal and non-eternal — as distinct [aspects]. That which is the prior eternal essential nature — in saying that the [entity] regarded as eternal perishes by itself afterwards — he asserts destruction at every single moment. Otherwise, by the reasoning stated above, destruction would be impossible even afterwards. But if its destruction does not occur at every moment, then it would be impossible afterwards as well, so he would be asserting perpetual non-destruction — and consequently, the cause of destruction would be powerless, utterly ineffectual, with regard to the prior essential nature regarded as eternal.

body.translated_text: The proponent of the established position says: "This twofold alternative just stated is not transcended." What kind of twofold alternative? 'Is the entity eternal?' and so forth. But surely, for one who accepts persistence for a limited time, there is no scope for the alternative of eternality. No. Even upon accepting that, eternality itself has been accepted. For consider: if this [entity] is produced by its own causes as having the property of persisting for a year, then at the end of the year, the essential nature by which it has persisted for a year — which was [its nature] at the very beginning, at the time of arising, as having the property of persisting for a year — that very [nature remains] even at the end [of the year]. Therefore it would persist for another year. And even at the end of that [second year], since the essential nature of the property of persisting for a year, [established] at the time of the first arising, has not been relinquished, there is the consequence of persistence for yet another year, and so even upon accepting the property of persistence for a limited time, eternality itself has been accepted — thus the alternative of eternality is inescapable. And since it is accepted that [the entity] ceases by itself in the presence of a cause of destruction, the alternative of non-eternality is [also entailed] — that is, the alternative of a perishable nature. For consider: when the essential nature of this [entity] that perishes by itself in the presence of what is regarded as the cause of destruction is the very same [nature] — since the entity has a single form — [as that] of what has just arisen, then the consequence of destruction at that very [moment of arising follows] — so how can its property of persisting for a limited time be possible? When the alternatives are thus posed, if the latter alternative is accepted, the persistence for a limited time itself is destroyed, so one must accept precisely the alternative of eternality. In that case, upon accepting that [the entity] perishes by itself in the presence of a cause of destruction, he says: 'having been eternal before, it afterwards becomes non-eternal, of a perishable nature.' "And in saying this, he also asserts a duality of entities." The word 'also' refers to what will be stated. (

body.text: nanu ca vināśahetornaiva sāmarthyamupagataṃ parena virodhisannidhimapekṣya svayaṃ nāśopagamāt | na | ata eva tannibandhanatvaprasaṅgāt nāśasya | anyathā hyakiñcitkaraḥ kimityasāvapekṣyate?, hetubhāvasyāpekṣālakṣaṇatvāt | svahetava evātrāparādhyanti yadakiñcitkare 'pi tatrāpekṣāyāṃ niyuñjata iti cet | kaḥ punarayamasthānābhiniveśaḥ teṣāṃ yat tatra tathā niyuñjate | tasmādupakāryapekṣāyāmeva hetavo niyuñjānāḥ śobhante | anyathā te 'pi kāryātmāno naiva tanniyogamādriyeran | kathaṃ cākiñcitkaro virodhī nāma? | na hyasyāvirodhitvābhimatādviśeṣaḥ kaściditi yatkiñcidetat |
body.translated_text: But the opponent has not accepted any efficacy of the cause of destruction at all, since [he holds that] destruction is accepted as occurring by itself in dependence on the presence of an opposing [factor]. No. For precisely this reason there is the consequence that destruction is contingent upon that [opposing factor]. Otherwise, why would that ineffectual [factor] be depended upon, since the very definition of being a cause is dependence [of the effect upon it]? If [one says] it is the [entity's] own causes that are at fault here, in that they appoint [the entity] to dependence even on something ineffectual — then what is this absurd insistence of theirs that they should appoint it thus? Therefore, causes are fitting only when they appoint [the entity] to dependence on what is beneficial [to the effect]. Otherwise, they too, being of the nature of effects [themselves], would not heed that appointment. And how can an opposing [factor] that is ineffectual be called 'opposing' at all? For there is no distinction between it and what is regarded as non-opposing — so all this is meaningless.

body.text: yadapyuktaṃ ‘yathānyeṣāṃ kṣaṇikavādināmakiñcitkaramapi mugdarādikamapekṣya ghaṭādipravāho nivartate tathāsmākamapi kālāntarasthāyī bhāvaḥ'; iti tadapi parasamayānabhijñatayocyate | yato nāsmākaṃ pravāho nāma kṣaṇavyatirikto 'sti yo 'kiñcitkaramugdarādisannidhau nivarteta | kṣaṇā eva hi kevalaṃ santi | te ca svanivṛttau na mugdarādikamapekṣante, svarasata eva nirodhāt | yā tu teṣāṃ kapālādivṛttilakṣaṇā paryudāsavṛttyā nivṛttiḥ yasyāṃ satyāmekatvābhiniveśino lokasya sadṛśāparabhāvarūpasya vibhramanimittasyāpagamāt ‘nivṛttā ghaṭādayaḥ'; iti vyavahāraḥ, tatrākiñcitkaratvaṃ mugdarādīnāṃ naivāsti, tadbhāva eva teṣāṃ bhāvāt | vegavanmugdarādisahakāriṇo ghaṭakṣaṇāt parasparopasarpaṇādyāśrayāt (

children.text: ) pratyayaviśeṣāt sañjātātiśayāt kapāladerbhavanadharmatvāt tasya ca tajjannasvabhāvatvāditi |
children.translated_text: ) from the special condition, having acquired an excellence, potsherds etc. have the property of coming into being, and since they are of a nature born from that [condition].

body.translated_text: As for what was said — 'just as for other <s>kṣaṇikavādins</s> (proponents of momentariness), the stream of pots etc. ceases in dependence on a hammer etc. that is [itself] ineffectual, so too for us an entity persisting for a limited time [ceases similarly]' — that too is said out of ignorance of the other's system. For according to us, there is no such thing as a 'stream' apart from the [individual] moments that would cease in the presence of an ineffectual hammer etc. There are simply individual moments alone. And they do not depend on a hammer etc. for their own cessation, since they cease by their very nature. But the cessation of those [moments] that takes the form of the exclusionary negation, characterized by the occurrence of potsherds etc. — in the presence of which, for the world that clings to unity, due to the disappearance of what is the cause of the illusion, namely the form of a similar subsequent [entity], the conventional usage 'pots etc. have ceased' [occurs] — in that regard, the hammer etc. are not at all ineffectual, since those [potsherds etc.] come into being precisely because of those [hammers etc.]. From the moment of the pot, [conjoined] with the auxiliary cause of a hammer etc. possessing velocity, through a special condition based on mutual proximity etc. (

body.text: svabhāvadvayopagamaprasaṅgāditi parijihīrṣayā para āha- "na prāg" ityādi | kuta etat? | "ekasvabhāvatvāt" | sarvadaikasvabhāvasya sarvadā nityataiva na paścādanityasvabhāvatāsambhava iti |
body.translated_text: Wishing to avoid the consequence of accepting a duality of essential natures, the opponent says: "Not previously" and so forth. Whence this? "Because of having a single essential nature." For that which always has a single essential nature is always eternal alone — the essential nature of non-eternality is impossible afterwards.

body.text: siddhāntavādyāha- "sa tarhi bhāvaḥ" sarvadā nityasvabhāvaḥ svabhāvena "nāśamanāviśan" apratipadyamānaḥ kathaṃ naiva naṣṭo(kathaṃ naṣṭo) nāma? | kutaḥ? "tatsvabhāvavināśayoḥ" nityasvabhāvatāyā, vināśasya cānityarūpatāyāśca "aparaspararūpatvāt" parasparaparihārarūpatvāt | upasaṃharannāha- "yata evaṃ" sthitidharmaṇāṃ vināśo naiva yujyate tasmāt sati asya vināśe yadyavaśyambhāvī kṛtakarūpasya sato vināśa iṣyate paraistadā "vināśasvabhāvena"- vinaśyati nāvatiṣṭhata iti vināśaḥ | kartari bahulavacanād ghañ | sa svabhāvo yasya tena vināśasvabhāvenāsthitidharmaṇā | "tena" kṛtakarūpeṇa satā vastunā svahetubhyo "bhavitavyam" anyathāvaśyambhāvitayopagatasya kṛtakātmanāṃ satāṃ vināśasyaivāyogāt |
body.translated_text: The proponent of the established position says: "That entity then," always having an eternal essential nature, "not undergoing" — not experiencing — "destruction" by its essential nature, how is it not destroyed (how is it destroyed) at all? Why? "Because the nature of that [entity] and destruction" — that is, [because] the eternal essential nature and destruction, which is of the form of non-eternality — "are not of each other's form" — are of the form of mutual exclusion. Summarizing, he says: "Since thus" destruction of entities with the property of persistence is simply not justified, therefore, if its destruction is [accepted] — that is, if the destruction of what exists as having a produced nature is accepted by the opponents as necessarily occurring — then "with a nature of destruction" — 'it perishes and does not persist' is destruction; the agent-noun suffix <s>ghañ</s> [is used] in the sense of the agent by the rule 'in many cases'; that which has that as its essential nature, i.e., with the nature of destruction, without the property of persistence — "by that" [entity] that exists as having a produced nature, "it must be" [so] from its own causes, since otherwise, for the destruction that is accepted as necessarily occurring for things of a produced nature, there would be no justification at all.

body.text: bhavatvevam iti cet | āha- "tathāpi" svayaṃ vināśasvabhāvatve 'pi na kevalamavinaśvarasvabhāvatve svabhāvānyathātvāsambhavād vyartho vināśaheturiti prathamavikalpopanyāsa evoktam na punarucyate | yata evaṃ "tena" ityādi sugamam |
body.translated_text: If [the opponent says] 'let it be so' — he says: "Even so," even when having the nature of destruction by itself, the mere [consequence] that the cause of destruction is futile when there is no non-perishable essential nature — since the essential nature cannot become otherwise — this is precisely the presentation of the first alternative that has already been stated, and need not be repeated. Since thus, "by that" and so forth is easily understood.

body.text: tadevaṃ vināśaṃ pratyanapekṣāmasāmarthya- vaiyarthyābhyāṃ taddhetvayogena kṛtakalakṣaṇasya sattvasya pūrvācāryadarśitāṃ pratipādya yathāsau viparyaye bādhakapramāṇatāmanubhavati tada darśayannāha- "tasmād vināśa" ityādi | prayogastvevam- ye yadbhāvaṃ pratyanapekṣāste tadbhāvaniyatāḥ | tadyathā- antyā kāraṇasāmagrī svakāryotpādane | anapekṣaśca kṛtakarūpaḥ san bhāvo vināśe 'vaśyambhāvivināśatayopagataḥ (

children.text: ) parairiti svabhāvahetuprasaṅgaprayogo viparyaye bādhakaṃ pramāṇaṃ pūrvācāryapradarśitam | "tataḥ" tadbhāvaniyatatve, nāśasyākādācitkatvādudayānantaraṃ nāśa iti "yaḥ san" kṛtakalakṣaṇo bhāvaḥ "sa vināśī" vinaśvarasvabhāvo naśvaratāyāḥ sādhyadharmasya nivṛttau ca kṛtakalakṣaṇasattvanivṛttiriti kṛtvā kṛtakalakṣaṇasya sattvasya kṣaṇikatāyāmanvayavyatirekasiddhiḥ sampadyate anapekṣayānukrāntasattvakṣaṇikatvayostādātmyasiddheḥ tannibandhanayoranvayavyatirekayorapi niścayāt |
children.translated_text: ) by the opponents — thus the formal argument through <s>svabhāvahetu</s> (essential-nature reason) constitutes, in the contrary case, a countervailing proof as demonstrated by the earlier masters. "Therefore" — given determination by the occurrence of that, and since destruction is not occasional, destruction [occurs] immediately after arising — "that which exists" — the entity characterized as produced — "is perishable," of a perishable essential nature. And upon the cessation of the property to be proved, namely perishability, the being-existent characterized as produced also ceases — thus the establishment of the <s>anvaya</s> (positive concomitance) and <s>vyatireka</s> (negative concomitance) of the momentariness of what is characterized as existent-and-produced is accomplished, because the identity of independence [with respect to destruction] and the momentariness of what is existent is established through their essential sameness, and because the <s>anvaya</s> and <s>vyatireka</s> grounded in that [identity] are also ascertained.

body.translated_text: Thus, having demonstrated in accordance with the earlier masters' view that, through the absence of dependence on [external factors] for destruction and through the powerlessness and futility [of destruction-causes], the being-existent nature of what is characterized as produced is without a cause of destruction, he now shows how that [argument] in the contrary case constitutes a <s>bādhaka-pramāṇa</s> (countervailing proof), saying: "Therefore, destruction" and so forth. The formal argument is as follows: Those that are independent with respect to the occurrence of something are determined by the occurrence of that [thing]. For example, the final aggregate of causes [is independent] with respect to the production of its own effect. And the entity that exists as having a produced nature is independent with respect to destruction, being accepted as necessarily perishable (

body.text: tadevaṃ pūrvācāryān prati akṛtakasya sato 'bhāvāt "sadakāraṇavannityam" iti nityalakṣaṇavirahādeva na tannityatvam | yattu sad utpattimat tad uktena nyāyenāvaśyaṃnāśitayopagataṃ paraiḥ kālāntarasthāyi na bhavatīti prati pāditam |
body.translated_text: Thus, with respect to the earlier masters, since there is no uncreated existent, "what is existent and without a cause is eternal" — by the very absence of the definition of eternality, its eternality does not hold. But that which is existent and has origination — it has been demonstrated by the stated reasoning that, being accepted by the opponents as necessarily perishable, it does not persist for a limited time.

body.text: 44. sāmānyena sattvakṣaṇikatvayostādātmyavyāptipradarśanam |
body.translated_text: 44. Demonstration of the <s>tādātmya-vyāpti</s> (identity-based pervasion) between existence and momentariness in general.

body.text: yadā tu yat sat tat kṣaṇikameveti sāmānyenocyate kṛtakākṛtakalakṣaṇaṃ sato bhedamanapekṣya prauḍhavāditayā kṛtakasyāpi cāvaśyambhāvī vināśa iti paropagamo nāpekṣyate, tadā vināśaṃ pratyanapekṣatvameva sarvasya na sidhyati | yeṣāṃ hi vināśo bhavaṃ(van) dṛṣṭo ghaṭādīnāṃ teṣāmeva taddhaitvayogat tatrānapekṣā yujyate | ye tu deśādivyavahitāḥ parvatādayo vā vinaśāmāviśanto na dṛṣṭāḥ teṣāmavaśyaṃ vināśitvopagamanibandhanābhāvādantye 'pyayaṃ vināśaṃ pratyanapekṣa eva vinaśyanna'viśeṣādādāvapi tadbhāvaniyata iti vaktumaśakyatvāt tatsvabhāvasāpekṣatvāt | vināśaṃ pratyanapekṣatvāsiddherakṛtakānāṃ cākāśādīnāṃ vināśisvabhāvasāpekṣāṇāmityanapekṣayā sato naśvarasvabhāvatāsiddheḥ anvayavyatirekayostannibandhanayorayogamutpaśyannarthakriyāvirodhalakṣaṇameva tadā bādhakaṃ pramāṇaṃ tādātmyaprasādhakamabhidhānīyamiti manyamānaḥ pūrvapakṣamutthāpayannāha- "svabhāvato" naśvaratve 'pyuktena (

children.text: ) nyāyena paridṛśyamānavināśānāṃ ghaṭādīnāṃ "kaścid" deśādivyavahitaḥ parvatādirvānupalabdhavināśaḥ kṛtako 'pi sadrūpa ākāśādirvākṛtakaḥ sanna "'tatsvabhāvo 'pi" avināśisvabhāvo 'pi syāt | apiśabdaḥ sambhāvanāyām | tasya vināśisvabhāvasaṃsādhakapramāṇābhāvādāśaṅkayata etat | tataśca vināśisvabhāvasāpekṣatvāt tadanapekṣatvamasiddhamiti tadvaśāt sādhyasya kṣaṇikatvasya sattvasvabhāvatvāsiddheḥ tannibandhanā nānvayavyatirekasiddhiriti | kiṃ punaratrāśaṅkānimittaṃ yena kaścidatatsvabhāvo 'pyāśaṅkayata ityāha- "na hi sarvaḥ sarvasya svabhāvaḥ" iti | vicitrasvabhāvā hi bhāvā dṛśyante- kecit sapratighāḥ kecidapratighāḥ, tathā nīlānīlādisvabhāvāḥ, tathā kecidvināśinaḥ anye tvavināśisvabhāvāḥ śaṅkayanta iti pūrvapakṣāśaṅkā |
children.translated_text: ) reasoning, "some" [entity] — separated by distance etc., such as a mountain, or one whose destruction has not been apprehended, even if produced, being of the nature of an existent, or like space etc., even if uncreated — being existent, "might not be of that essential nature" — might not be of a perishable essential nature. The word 'api' (even) is in the sense of possibility. This is suspected because of the absence of a proof that would establish its perishable essential nature. And consequently, since [the argument] depends on a perishable essential nature, the independence [with respect to destruction] is unestablished, and by virtue of that, since the identity of the property to be proved — momentariness — with the essential nature of existence is unestablished, there is no establishment of <s>anvaya</s> and <s>vyatireka</s> grounded in that. What then is the basis for this suspicion, such that 'some [entity] might not be of that essential nature' is suspected? He says: "For not every [property] is the essential nature of everything." For entities are seen to have diverse essential natures: some are resistant, some non-resistant; likewise, some have the essential nature of blue, some of non-blue; likewise, some are perishable, while others are suspected of having a non-perishable essential nature — thus the prima facie suspicion.

body.translated_text: But when it is stated generally that 'whatever is existent is momentary,' without regard to the distinction between produced and unproduced characteristics of what is existent, and in a bold manner — and when even the opponent's acceptance that 'destruction is necessarily [entailed] for the produced' is not relied upon — then the independence with respect to destruction of everything cannot be established. For only those things such as pots etc. whose destruction has been observed have justifiable independence with respect to that [destruction], due to the absence of a cause of destruction for them. But those that are separated by distance etc., such as mountains, or that are not seen undergoing destruction — for them, since there is no basis for accepting their perishable nature, and since the final [entity] too 'perishes independently with respect to destruction, and since there is no distinction [between it and the earlier ones], it is determined by the occurrence of that even at the beginning' — this cannot be stated, because it depends on the very essential nature of perishability. Since the independence with respect to destruction is unestablished, and since for uncreated [entities] such as space etc. which depend on a perishable essential nature — through this independence the perishable essential nature of what is existent is unestablished — seeing the impossibility of the <s>anvaya</s> and <s>vyatireka</s> grounded in that, and thinking that at that point a countervailing proof characterized by the contradiction with <s>arthakriyā</s> (causal efficacy) alone, which establishes identity [between existence and momentariness], should be stated, he raises the prima facie objection saying: "By essential nature" — even when perishability [is accepted], by the stated (

body.text: na- ‘kaścidatatsvabhāvo 'pi syāt'- iti āśaṅkanīyam, tathābhāve hyakṣaṇikatvaṃ tasya syāt | tasmiṃśca satyavastutvaprasaṅgāt kuto 'tatsvabhāvatāśaṅkā? | kathaṃ punarakṣaṇikatve 'vastutvaprasaṅgaḥ? | yataḥ sattvasya kṣaṇikatvasvabhāvatayānvayavyatirekasiddhirityata āha- "śaktirhi" ityādi |
body.translated_text: One should not suspect that 'something might exist that does not have that nature [i.e., momentariness],' for if it were so, it would be non-momentary. And if that [non-momentariness] were the case, since there would be the unwanted consequence of it being a real entity, whence the suspicion of its not having that nature? But how is there the unwanted consequence of non-reality in the case of non-momentariness? Because the establishment of <s>sattva</s> (existence) through co-presence and co-absence is due to its having the nature of momentariness — therefore he says "<s>śakti</s> (capacity) indeed" and so forth.

body.text: 45. arthakriyākāritvameva sattvaṃ, tacca kṣaṇikānāmeveti |
body.translated_text: 45. <s>Arthakriyākāritva</s> (causal efficacy) alone is <s>sattva</s> (existence), and that belongs only to momentary entities.

body.text: evaṃ manyate- iha tāvadidameva vicāraṇīyam kiṃlakṣaṇametad bhāvānāṃ sattvaṃ yuktamiti | tatra na sattāyogalakṣaṇamavyāpteḥ, sāmānyadiṣvabhāvāt | vandhyāsutādiṣvapi bhāvād ativyāptervā | vandhyāsutādīnāmasattvāt kathaṃ sattāyogaḥ? iti cet | na | itaretarāśrayāt | yatasteṣāmasattvaṃ sattāyogavirahādeva tadvirahaścāsattvāditi | yadi ca satāmeva sattāyogaḥ evaṃ tarhyanyat sattvalakṣaṇamabhidhānīyam sattāyogasya ca vaiyarthyam, tat eva vastunaḥ sattvāt | sarvārthakriyāsāmarthyavirahāt sattāyogābhāvasteṣāmiti (

children.translated_text: Hbṭ 146

children.text: ) cet | evaṃ sati yadevārthakriyasāmarthyayuktaṃ tasyaiva sattāyoga ityarthakriyāsāmarthyameva bhāvalakṣaṇamāyātamityapārthakaḥ | sattāyogaḥ | "itthaṃ ca" evam | anyathā sāmānyādīnāṃ kathaṃ svarūpaṃ sattvaṃ syāt? | arthakriyāsāmarthyaṃ tu sarveṣāmastīti tadeva bhāvalakṣaṇam |
children.translated_text: — if so, then connection with <s>sattā</s> belongs only to that which possesses <s>arthakriyāsāmarthya</s> (capacity for causal efficacy), and thus <s>arthakriyāsāmarthya</s> alone turns out to be the defining characteristic of entities — hence the connection with <s>sattā</s> is pointless. "And thus" — in this way. Otherwise, how could <s>sāmānya</s> (universals) and the like have <s>sattva</s> (existence) as their own nature? But <s>arthakriyāsāmarthya</s> (capacity for causal efficacy) belongs to all [real entities], therefore that alone is the defining characteristic of entities.

body.translated_text: He thinks thus: Here, first of all, this alone is to be investigated — what characterization of <s>sattva</s> (existence) of entities is proper? In that regard, it is not characterized by connection with <s>sattā</s> (the universal 'existence'), because of non-pervasion, since it is absent in <s>sāmānya</s> (universals) and the like. Or because of over-extension, since it would be present even in the son of a barren woman and such [fictions]. If one objects: how can there be connection with <s>sattā</s> for the son of a barren woman and the like, since they are non-existent? No, because of mutual dependence. For their non-existence is only due to the absence of connection with <s>sattā</s>, and that absence [of connection with <s>sattā</s>] is due to their non-existence. And if connection with <s>sattā</s> belongs only to what is real, then some other definition of <s>sattva</s> must be stated, and the connection with <s>sattā</s> becomes pointless, since that alone [already] constitutes the reality of a thing. If one says: the absence of connection with <s>sattā</s> for those [fictions] is due to the absence of all <s>arthakriyāsāmarthya</s> (capacity for causal efficacy) —

body.text: "utpādavyavyaghnauvyayuktaṃ sat" ityetadapyayuktam, dhrauvyeṇotpādavyayayorvirodhāt ekasmiṃ(smin) dharmiṇyayogāt | kathañcidutpādavyayau kathañcit dhrauvyamiti cet | yathotpādavyayau na tathā dhrauvyam, yathā ca dhrauvyaṃ na tathotpādavyayāviti naikaṃ vastu yathoktalakṣaṇaṃ syāt | tato 'nyasya bhāvalakṣaṇasyāyogāt śakteścāntaśaḥ svajñānajanane 'pyupagamāt paraiḥ, anyathā ṣaṭpadārthādivyavasthānāyogāt saiva bhāvalakṣaṇam, sarvaśaktivirahaḥ punarabhāvalakṣaṇam |
body.translated_text: The [Jain] definition "that which is endowed with origination, destruction, and permanence is <s>sat</s> (real)" is also improper, because permanence contradicts origination and destruction, [and hence] they cannot co-occur in a single substratum. If one says: origination and destruction in one respect, permanence in another respect — then in the respect in which there is origination and destruction, there is no permanence, and in the respect in which there is permanence, there is no origination and destruction; thus no single entity would have the stated definition. Therefore, since no other defining characteristic of entities is tenable, and since even the opponents accept <s>śakti</s> (capacity) at the very least in the production of its own cognition — otherwise the systematic arrangement of the six categories and so forth would be untenable — that [capacity] alone is the defining characteristic of entities, while the absence of all capacity is the defining characteristic of non-entities.

body.text: sarvagrahaṇaṃ ca sarvasya vastuno vastvantaraśaktiviraharūpatvādabhāvatānirāsārtham | yasya tu na kvacicchaktiḥ sa evaikāntenābhāva ucyate |
body.translated_text: The word 'all' [in 'absence of all capacity'] is used to prevent [the unwanted consequence of] non-existence [being attributed to real things], since every real entity lacks the capacity for [producing] other entities [i.e., not everything can produce everything]. But that which has no capacity whatsoever with respect to anything — that alone is definitively called a non-entity.

body.text: śaktilakṣaṇameva sattvamakṣaṇike syāt tataḥ kṣaṇikātmatā sattvasya na sidhyatīti kuto 'nvayavyatirekau? iti cet, āha- "na caivākṣaṇikasya" kvacit kārye 'ntaśo jñānalakṣaṇe 'pi śaktirasti tat kutastasya tallakṣaṇaṃ sattvamatītāderiva bhaviṣyati?, yataḥ sattvasya kṣaṇikātmatā na sidhyet |
body.translated_text: If one objects: the <s>sattva</s> (existence) characterized by capacity might exist in a non-momentary entity, and therefore the momentary nature of <s>sattva</s> would not be established — so whence co-presence and co-absence? — he replies: "And indeed a non-momentary entity" has no capacity with respect to any effect, not even one characterized by cognition. So how could it possess <s>sattva</s> characterized by that [capacity], any more than a past entity and the like could? For [if it could,] the momentary nature of <s>sattva</s> would not be established.

body.text: nanu ca śakteratīndriyatvāt kāraṇānāṃ kāryarambhaniyamābhāvācca kathaṃ tadviraho 'kṣaṇikasya bhavet yato 'sya sarvaśaktivirahalakṣaṇenāsattvena virodhinā nirākriyamāṇaṃ sattvaṃ kṣaṇikātmatāmevānubhavet yato 'nvayavyatirekau syātāmityata āha- "kramayaugapadyābhyām" ityādi | naiva pratyakṣataḥ kāryavirahādvā sarvaśaktiviraho 'kṣaṇikatve ucyate, kintu tavdyāpakavirahāt | tathā hi- kramayaugapadyābhyāṃ kāryakriyā vyāptā prakārāntarābhāvāt | tataḥ kāryakriyāśaktivyāpakayostayorakṣaṇikatve (

children.translated_text: Hbṭ 147

children.text: ) virodhāt nirvṛttestavdyāptāyāḥ kāryakriyāśakterapi nivṛttiriti sarvaśaktivirahalakṣaṇamasattvamakṣaṇikatve vyāpakānupalabdhirākarṣati, viruddhayorekatrāyogāt | tato nivṛttaṃ sattvaṃ kṣaṇikeṣvevāvatiṣṭhamānaṃ tadātmatāmanubhavatīti- ‘yat sat tat kṣaṇikameva'; ityanvayavyatirekarūpāyā vyāpteḥ siddhirniścayo bhavati |
children.translated_text: from the cessation of those [two], there is also cessation of the capacity for producing effects that is pervaded by them. Thus, non-existence characterized by the absence of all capacity is established for non-momentariness through the non-apprehension of the pervader, since contradictory [properties] cannot co-occur in a single locus. Therefore, <s>sattva</s> (existence), having departed [from non-momentary entities], abiding only in momentary entities, is experienced as having their nature — thus 'whatever is real is momentary alone.' In this way, the establishment — that is, the ascertainment — of <s>vyāpti</s> (pervasion) in the form of co-presence and co-absence is achieved.

body.translated_text: But [the opponent objects:] since capacity is beyond the senses, and since there is no fixed rule that causes must [always visibly] initiate effects, how can the absence of that [capacity] in a non-momentary entity be established, such that its <s>sattva</s> (existence), being negated by its contradictory — namely non-existence characterized by the absence of all capacity — would entail momentary nature alone, so that co-presence and co-absence would follow? Therefore he says "by succession and simultaneity" and so forth. The absence of all capacity in the case of non-momentariness is not asserted [merely] from direct perception or from the absence of effects, but rather from the absence of what pervades [capacity]. For thus: the production of effects is pervaded by <s>krama</s> (succession) and <s>yaugapadya</s> (simultaneity), since there is no third alternative. Therefore, since <s>krama</s> and <s>yaugapadya</s>, which pervade the capacity for producing effects, contradict non-momentariness,

body.text: nanu ca prakārāntarābhāvāt kāryamaṅkurādikaṃ bījādinā kramayaugapadyābhyāmeva kriyata ityucyate sa eva tu prakārāntaravirahaḥ kāryātmanaḥ kutaḥ siddhaḥ? | prakārāntarasyopalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptatve kathamatyantāsambhavaḥ? | kevalaṃ deśādiniṣedhamātrameva syāt | anupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptatvenāsattāniścayo viprakarṣiṇāmiti kutastadabhāvasiddhiḥ? | tataḥ prakarāntareṇārthakriyāsambhavāt kramayaugapadyanivṛttāvapi nārthakriyāsāmarthyanivṛttiriti kuto 'kṣaṇikatve sati sarvasāmarthyavirahalakṣaṇamasattvam?, yataḥ sattvasya kṣanikātmatayānvayavyatirekau syātām? | na | ubhayathāpyadoṣāt | tathā hi- kramo nāma paripāṭiḥ kāryāntarāsāhityaṃ kaivalyamaṅkurādeḥ, yaugapadyamapi tasyāparairbbījādikāryaiḥ sāhityaṃ | prakārāntaraṃ cāṅkurādeḥ tadubhayāvasthāvirahe 'pyanyathābhavanam | tasya cāṅkurādisvabhāvasyānyasahitasya kevalasya vābhāve pratyakṣabodhagamyamāne satyupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta eva svabhāvaḥ kramayaugapadyabhāvabahirbhūto nopalabhyate | vastunaḥ upalabhyasyānyasāhitye kaivalye cāpanīte tadviviktadeśādipratibhāsinaḥ pratyakṣasyodayāt svabhāvānupalambhata evābhāvaniścayādilakṣaṇavyavahāravṛtteḥ | tasya cāṅkurādibhāvasyāvasthādvayabahirbhāvaniṣedhe kayościddeśakālayoḥ deśāntarādau krameṇāṅkurādibhāvavatīratarasmin vā bhāve 'pi na kācit kṣatiḥ | tataḥ pratyakṣata eva prakārāntarābhāvasiddheḥ kathaṃ kramayaugapadyābhyāmarthakriyāśaktiravyāptā syāt? | śāstrakārastu yathā pratyakṣata eva prakārāntarābhāvasiddhiḥ tathā svayam "etena kramākramādayo 'pī"ti atidiśan vakṣyati |
body.translated_text: But [the opponent says:] it is stated that the effect such as a sprout is produced by a seed and the like only through succession and simultaneity, because there is no third alternative — but how is that very absence of a third alternative established with respect to the effect? If a third alternative were such as to fulfill the conditions for apprehension, how could it be absolutely impossible? There would only be a negation limited to [particular] place and so forth. Since for those [alternatives] that are remote, the ascertainment of non-existence is due to the fulfillment of the conditions for non-apprehension, whence the establishment of its absence? Therefore, since causal efficacy is possible through a third alternative, even when succession and simultaneity are negated, there would be no negation of <s>arthakriyāsāmarthya</s> (capacity for causal efficacy) — so how, given non-momentariness, could there be non-existence characterized by the absence of all capacity, such that co-presence and co-absence of <s>sattva</s> with momentary nature would follow? No, because there is no fault in either case. For thus: <s>krama</s> (succession) means serial order — the separateness, the singularity of a sprout and the like without accompaniment by other effects; and <s>yaugapadya</s> (simultaneity) is its accompaniment by other effects of the seed and the like. A third alternative would be the existence of the sprout and the like in some other way even when both those states are absent. But when the nature of the sprout and the like — whether accompanied by others or alone — is absent, and this absence is accessible to direct perceptual awareness, then the nature [supposedly] outside of the states of succession and simultaneity fulfills precisely the conditions for apprehension yet is not apprehended. Since, when the accompaniment by others and the singularity of a real apprehensible entity are removed, direct perception arises that manifests [only] the place and so forth devoid of that [entity], the ascertainment of absence and related conventional usage proceed from the very non-apprehension of that nature. And when the existence of the sprout and the like is negated outside the two states, there is no harm even if in some particular place and time the sprout-nature proceeds by succession, or even if it exists [simultaneously with other effects]. Therefore, since the absence of a third alternative is established by direct perception itself, how could the capacity for causal efficacy through succession and simultaneity be unpervasive? The author of the treatise [<s>Dharmakīrti</s>] himself, showing how the absence of a third alternative is established by direct perception itself, will extend this by saying "By this, succession, non-succession, and so forth are also [covered]."

body.text: anupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptatve 'pi prakārāntarasya kramayaugapadyayoranyo 'nyavya vacchedarūpatvādevāśrayasi (devābhāvasi)ddhi tathāhi- anyonyavyavacchedarūpāṇāmekaniṣedhenāparavidhānāt tasyāpratiṣedhe vidhipratiṣedhayorvirodhādubhayapratiṣedhātmanaḥ prakārāntarasya kutaḥ sambhavaḥ? | atra prayogaḥ- yatra yatprakāravyavacchedena yaditaraprakāravyavasthānaṃ na tatra prakārāntarasambhavaḥ, tadyathānīlaprakāravyavacchedenānīlaprakārāntaravyavasthāyāṃ pīte | asti ca kramayaugapadyayoranyataraprakāravyavacchedena taditaraprakāravyavasthānaṃ vyavacchidyamānaprakārāviṣayīkṛte sarvatra kāryakāraṇarūpe vastunīti viruddhopalabdhiḥ vyavacchidyamānaprakāretaravyavasthānaṃ ca, prakārāntarasambhavaśca tato bahirbhāvalakṣaṇa ityanayostattvānyatvarūpayoranyonyaparihārasthitalakṣaṇatvāt | na cātrāpi bādhakāntarāśaṅkayānavasthānamāśaṅkanīyam, pūrvaprasiddhasya virodhasya smaraṇamātratvāt | viruddhopalabdhiṣu bahirddharmiṇi hetoḥ sadbhāvamupadarśya virodhasādhanameva bādhakam, taccehāsti | tato viruddhayorekatrāsambhāvāt pratiyogyabhāvaniścayaḥ śītoṣṇasparśayoriva bhāvābhāvayoriva veti kuto 'navasthā? |
body.translated_text: Even when a third alternative fulfills the conditions for apprehension, [its impossibility] is established precisely because succession and simultaneity have the nature of mutual exclusion. For thus: since among things that are of the nature of mutual exclusion, the negation of one entails the establishment of the other, and since [given] the non-negation of that [other], there would be a contradiction between affirmation and negation, whence the possibility of a third alternative that is the negation of both? Here the formal argument is: wherever there is the establishment of one alternative mode by the exclusion of another mode, there is no possibility of a third alternative — as, for example, in the case of yellow, which is established as the non-blue alternative mode by the exclusion of the blue mode. And there is indeed, in the case of succession and simultaneity, the establishment of one alternative mode by the exclusion of the other, with respect to every entity in the form of cause and effect that is not the object of the mode being excluded — this is an apprehension of the contradictory. And the establishment of the alternative to the excluded mode, and the possibility of a third alternative outside of it — these two, having the nature of identity and otherness respectively, are characterized by mutual exclusion. Nor should one suspect an infinite regress here due to the apprehension of some other defeater, since this is merely the recollection of a previously established contradiction. In apprehensions of the contradictory, having demonstrated the existence of the reason in the external subject, the very proof of contradiction serves as the defeater, and that is present here. Therefore, since contradictories cannot co-occur in a single locus, there is ascertainment of the absence of the counter-correlate — just as with cold and hot sensations, or with existence and non-existence — so whence an infinite regress?

body.text: tatra na krameṇākṣaṇikaḥ kāryāṇi karotyaviśeṣādakārakāvasthāyāmiva | sahakāryapekṣā ca dvividhasyāpi sahakāritvasyāyogādanupanyasanīyā | sarveṣāṃ caikakriyākāla eva kriyāprasakteḥ, tatkārakasya svabhāvasya tadaiva bhāvāt | nāpi yugapat, pratyakṣādivirodhāt, punastatkriyāprasaṅgācca | kṛtatvānneti cet, na, sāmarthyānapāyāt | anyathā prāgapyakārakarūpaviśeṣādakriyā syāt | kṛtasya kartumaśakyatvāditi cet | śaktāśaktatayā tarhyekatraiva kārye bhedaprasaṅga śālikodravabījāderiva | nityaśca yadā yugapat karoti tataḥ prāgapi bhāvāt tadaiva tatkriyāprasaṅgaḥ punastato 'pi pūrvataram ityevaṃ na kadācidyugapat kriyā syāt | pūrvottarakālayoścaikadā yugapatkāriṇo 'nyadā sarvārthakriyāsāmarthyavirahalakṣaṇamasattvaṃ (

children.translated_text: Hbṭ 149

children.text: ) syāditi kathaṃ na kṣaṇikatā? | kriyopagame vā kramapakṣa eva | tatra cokto doṣaḥ | evamakṣaṇikatve sati cakṣurādyāyatanānāmasattvaprasaṅgāt kṣaṇikatāyāmeva sattvamiti yat sat tat kṣaṇikameveti sato naśvarātmatāsiddheḥ anvayavyatirekarūpavyāptisiddhiriti ||
children.translated_text: how could it not be momentary? Or, if production is accepted, it falls only under the alternative of succession, and the fault stated there [applies]. Thus, since non-momentariness entails the unwanted consequence of non-existence for the sense faculties such as the eye and the like, <s>sattva</s> (existence) belongs only to what is momentary. Therefore, 'whatever is real is momentary alone' — since the perishable nature of what exists is established, the establishment of <s>vyāpti</s> (pervasion) in the form of co-presence and co-absence is achieved.

body.translated_text: In that regard, a non-momentary entity does not produce effects through succession, since there is no distinguishing feature [between the supposed productive moment and] the state of non-production — [it is the same at all times]. And the expectation of auxiliary causes should not be introduced, since neither type of auxiliary causation is tenable [for a permanent entity]. And since all [effects] would have to be produced at the very time of [the first] action, because the nature that is the producer exists at that very time. Nor [does a non-momentary entity produce effects] simultaneously, because this contradicts direct perception and other [means of knowledge], and because there would be the unwanted consequence of producing those [effects] again. If one says: it does not [produce again] because [the effect] has already been produced — no, because its capacity has not departed. Otherwise, even previously, there should be non-production due to there being no distinguishing feature in the form of a non-producing [state]. If one says: because what has been produced cannot be produced again — then, due to [the permanent entity being] capable and incapable with respect to one and the same effect, there would be the unwanted consequence of a division [in its nature], just as with rice seeds and millet seeds and the like [which are different entities producing different effects]. And since the permanent entity, whenever it produces simultaneously, existed even before that, there would be the unwanted consequence of producing those effects at that very [earlier] time, and even earlier than that — and thus simultaneous production would never occur. Since at earlier and later times, the entity that supposedly produces simultaneously at one time would have non-existence characterized by the absence of all <s>arthakriyāsāmarthya</s> (capacity for causal efficacy) at other times,

body.text: 3. kāryakāraṇabhāvavyavasthā |]
body.translated_text: [3. The determination of the cause-effect relation.]

body.text: tadevaṃ svabhāvahetau tādātmyasiddhinibandhanamanvayavyatirekaniścayaṃ pratipādya kāryahetau kāryakāraṇabhāvasiddhinimittatvāt tayostasyāśca pratyakṣānupalambhanibandhanāyāḥ prāgeva darśitatvāt tagdatamaparamapi pareṣāṃ bhrāntikāraṇapanetuṃ tadviṣayaṃ darśayannāha- "arthāntare" hetorvyatirikte vastuni gamye "kāryaṃ hetuḥ" | anarthāntare tu svabhāvo heturityuktam | kasmāt punararthāntare kāryameva heturityāha- "avyabhicārāt" iti kāryameva hyarthāntaraṃ na vyabhicarati nānyat yathoktaṃ prāk tataḥ kāryamevārthāntare gamye heturucyate saṃyogavaśāgdamakatve |
body.translated_text: Thus, having demonstrated the ascertainment of co-presence and co-absence, which is grounded in the establishment of essential identity in the case of the <s>svabhāvahetu</s> (essential-nature reason), now regarding the <s>kāryahetu</s> (effect reason) — since it is grounded in the establishment of the cause-effect relation, and since that [relation] is grounded in direct perception and non-apprehension, which have already been shown previously — in order to remove the additional cause of confusion for opponents regarding this further [topic], he presents the subject matter saying: "In a different entity" — that is, in a real thing that is distinct from the reason, the object to be inferred — "the effect is the reason." But in the case of a non-different entity, the reason is the essential nature, as has been stated. Why is it that only the effect is the reason regarding a different entity? He says: "Because of non-deviation" — for only the effect does not deviate from a different entity, and nothing else does, as was stated before. Therefore, only the effect is called the reason when a different entity is the object to be inferred, [provided there is] no dependence on [mere] association.

body.text: "na ca kenacit" ityādinā yaḥ sarvathā gamyagamakabhāvaprasaṅga ācāryeṇoktaḥ parasya, tamihāpi kāryahetau paraḥ kadācit prasañjayedityāśaṅkamāna āha- "kāryakāraṇa- " ityādi | yadi hi kāryaṃ heturucyate tadā kāryakāraṇabhāvena kāraṇenāsya gamakatvam | tathā ca sati sarvathā gamyagamakabhāvaḥ prāpnoti | agneḥ sāmānyadharmavad viśeṣadharmā api tārṇapārṇādayo gamyāḥ syuḥ | dhūmasyāpi viśeṣadharmavad dravyatvapārthivatvādayo 'pi sāmānyadharmā gamakā bhaveyuḥ | kutaḥ? "sarvathā janyajanakabhāvāt" | janyajanakabhāvo hi kāryakāraṇabhāva ucyate | sa ca nāgnidhūmayoraṃśena api tu sarveṇa prakāreṇa | tathāhi- yathā agniragnitvadravyatvasattvādibhiḥ sāmānyadharmairjanakaḥ tathā tārṇapārṇatvādibhirviśeṣadharmairapi, yathā ca dhūmo dhūmatvapāṇḍutvādibhiḥ svaniyatairviśeṣadharmairjanyaḥ tathā sāmānyadharmairapi sattvadravyatvādibhiḥ | tataśca yathā tayoḥ kāryakāraṇabhāvaḥ tathaiva gamyagamakabhāvaḥ prāpnoti, tasyaiva tannibandhanatvāditi pūrvapakṣāśaṅkā | atrāha- "na sarvathā janyajanakabhāvaḥ" tataśca kutastathā gamyagamakabhāvaḥ syāt? | kasmāt? iti cet, (

children.translated_text: Hbṭ 151

children.text: ) "tadabhāve" teṣāṃ tārṇapārṇatvādināṃ viśeṣadharmāṇāmabhāve "bhavato" dhūmamātrasya tebhya eva viśeṣadharmebhyo bhavatīti evamātmanaḥ "tadutpattiniyamasyābhāvāt" | tathā "tadabhāve" agnyabhāve bhavato dravyatvādeḥ sāmānyadharmasyāgnerevāyaṃ bhavatī tyevaṃrūpasya tadutpattiniyamasyābhāvāt kutaḥ sarvathā janyajanakabhāvaḥ?, yataḥ sarvathā gamyagamakabhāvaḥ syāt | na hyasati tadutpattiniyame janyajanakabhāvo vyavasthāpayituṃ yuktaḥ | yata evaṃ "tasmāt kāryaṃ" dhūmādikaṃ "svabhāvairyāvadbhi" rdhūmatvādibhiḥ svagataiḥ | itthambhūtalakṣaṇā ca tṛtīyā | "avīnābhāvi" vinā na bhavati | kairvinā na bhavati? | ‘kāraṇe yāvadbhiḥ svabhāvaiḥ'; ityatrāpi sambadhyate | kāraṇāśritairyāvadbhiḥ svabhāvairvinā te kāryagatāḥ svabhāvā na bhavanti hetuḥ taisteṣāmiti gamyate | kva avinābhāvi? | "kāraṇe" kāraṇaviṣaye aparo 'rthaḥ "kāraṇe" ādhārasaptamī | idānīṃ kāraṇasthaiḥ svabhāvairyāvadbhiragnitvadravyatvādibhiravinābhāvi teṣāṃ kāraṇagatānāṃ sāmānyadharmāṇāṃ hetuḥ kāryaṃ gamakam | kasmāt? ityāha- "tatkāryatvaniyamāt" teṣāmeva kāraṇagatānāṃ sāmānyadharmānāṃ tat kāryamityevaṃrūpasya niyamasya sadbhāvāt | nahi tān sāmānyadharmān kadācidapi kāryaṃ vyabhicarati |
children.translated_text: ) "In the absence of those" — in the absence of the particular properties such as being made of grass, having leaves, and the like — "of that which exists" — of mere smoke — from those very particular properties, the invariable rule of its production being of such a nature — "because of the absence of the invariable rule of its production from those." Likewise, "in the absence of that" — in the absence of fire — of the general properties such as substance-hood and the like that exist [even without fire] — the invariable rule of production of the form 'this arises only from fire' — because of the absence of such an invariable rule of production, how can there be in every respect a producer-produced relationship, since there would [then] be in every respect an inferential relationship? For in the absence of an invariable rule of production from that, it is not appropriate to establish a producer-produced relationship. Since it is thus, "therefore the effect" — smoke and the like — "by whatever natures" — smoke-hood and the like, which are its own — the instrumental case has the sense of characterizing a manner of being — "is inseparable from" — does not exist without. Without what does it not exist? This connects with 'by whatever natures belonging to the cause' as well. By whatever natures residing in the cause — without those, the natures belonging to the effect do not exist — this is the reason — by those [natures], those [effect-natures] are understood. In relation to what is it inseparable? "In the cause" — in the domain of the cause; another meaning: "in the cause" — locative of support. Now, [the effect] being inseparable from whatever natures — fire-hood, substance-hood, and the like — residing in the cause, is the indicator of those general properties belonging to the cause, being their effect. Why? He says: "Because of the invariable rule of being the effect of those" — because of the existence of the invariable rule of the form 'it is the effect of those very general properties belonging to the cause.' For never does the effect deviate from those general properties.

body.translated_text: With "and not by anything" and so forth, the <s>Ācārya</s> [<s>Dharmakīrti</s>] stated to the opponent the unwanted consequence of an all-encompassing relation of indicated and indicator. Anticipating that the opponent might raise the same [objection] here too regarding the <s>kāryahetu</s> (effect reason), he says: "cause and effect" and so forth. For if the effect is called the reason, then its capacity to indicate is through the cause-effect relation with the cause. And that being so, an all-encompassing relation of indicated and indicator would follow. The specific properties of fire such as being associated with grass, leaves, and so forth would be inferable just like its general properties. And the general properties of smoke such as being a substance, being earthly, and so forth would also serve as indicators just like its specific properties. Why? "Because the producer-produced relation obtains in every respect." For the producer-produced relation is called the cause-effect relation. And this [relation] between fire and smoke is not partial but obtains in every respect. For thus: just as fire is a producer through its general properties such as fire-nature, substance-hood, existence, and so forth, so too through its specific properties such as being associated with grass, leaves, and so forth; and just as smoke is a product through its specific properties such as smoke-nature, pale color, and so forth, which are unique to it, so too through its general properties such as existence, substance-hood, and the like. Therefore, just as there is a cause-effect relation between the two, so too should there be a relation of indicated and indicator, since the latter is grounded in the former — this is the prima facie objection. To this he replies: "The producer-produced relation does not obtain in every respect." And therefore, how could such a relation of indicated and indicator obtain? If asked: why? —

body.text: evaṃ kāraṇagatamaṃśaṃ pāścātyenārthena nirūpya prāktanenārthena kāryagatamaṃśaṃ nirūpayannāha- "taireva ca" ityādi | kāryamapi taireva dharmaiḥ svagataiḥ kāraṇagatānāṃ dharmāṇāṃ gamakam yathāntarā sambhavino dhūmatvapāṇḍupārṇatvādayo viśeṣarūpāstaiḥ kāraṇagataiḥ sāmānyadharmairvinā na bhavanti | atrāpi ‘tatkāryatvaniyamāt'; ityapekṣyate | teṣāmeva kāryagatānāṃ viśeṣadharmāṇāṃ kāraṇagatasāmānyadharmāpekṣayā kāryatvaniyamāt | na hi te viśeṣadharmāḥ kāryagatāḥ kāraṇasthasāmānyadharmairvinā kadācidapi bhavanti | tatasteṣāmeva kāryatvaniyamaḥ, nānyeṣāṃ dravyatvādīnāṃ (
