"tadatadrūpayoḥ" tasya tadanyavastuno yadrūpaṃ pratiniyataṃ sakalatrailokyavilakṣaṇaṃ yaccātadrūpaṃ tadrūpaṃ na bhavati pararūpaṃ tayoḥ "avivekād" avivecanād vivekenāvyavasthāpanādasāṅkaryeṇāprasādhanāt | sakalapararūpāsaṅkirṇaṃ hi tadrūpam taccet tatsāmarthyabhāvinā pratyakṣeṇa tathā nānukṛtaṃ kevalaṃ sammugdhākārameva tadutpannaṃ tadā kathantena tatparicchedaḥ syāt? | na hi yadrūpaṃ yadvastu tadrūpānanukāriṇā jñānena tatparicchedo yukto yathā- śukuśaṅkharūpānanukāriṇā kāmalinaḥ pītaśaṅkhāvabhāsinā jñāneneti | pratiniyatarūpānukāre vā tatparicchedasya kathamanyāvyavacchedo nāma? | tataḥ pratiniyatarūpānanukārādeva tadanyāvyavacchedaḥ | tathā ca tatparicchedābhāva iti |
body.translated_text: And necessarily the apprehension of <s>anyabhāva</s> (existence of something else) is itself the apprehension of <s>tadabhāva</s> (absence of that). Therefore, showing that neither for the purpose of avoiding confusion among real entities nor for the purpose of the practical usage "this does not exist here" is there justification for postulating a separate means of knowledge for absence (<s>abhāvapramāṇa</s>), he says: "Otherwise" — if it is not accepted that the apprehension of that is itself the apprehension of the absence of that — then "in the non-exclusion" (<s>avyavaccheda</s>), i.e. the non-elimination, i.e. the non-cognition of the absence, "of that which is other" — having a nature different from the other entity — through the ascertainment of the own-nature of "that" other entity, "the ascertainment of that itself would not be possible" — there would be no cognition of the own-nature of that other entity. What is the reason? Because of "the non-discrimination" (<s>aviveka</s>) "of its tadrūpa and atadrūpa" — that is, of the own-form of that other entity, which is determinate and distinct from everything in the three worlds, and the non-own-form, which is not that form but the form of others — because of the non-differentiation, the non-establishment through discrimination, the non-proof without admixture. For the own-form is unmixed with all other forms; if direct perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>), arising from the capacity of that [object], does not reproduce it as such, but arises merely in a confused form, then how could there be ascertainment of that through it? Indeed, the ascertainment of a thing whose form is such-and-such is not justified by a cognition that does not reproduce that form — just as the cognition of one with jaundice, which appears as a yellow conch-shell and does not reproduce the form of the white conch. Or if [you say] there is reproduction of the determinate form, then how can there be non-exclusion of the other? Therefore, from the very non-reproduction of the determinate form, there would be non-exclusion of the other. And thus there would be no ascertainment of that [entity].

body.text: bhavatyevaṃ tataḥ ko doṣaḥ? ityata āha- "ya eṣa vyavahāraḥ" sarvajanapratitaḥ "kasyacid" agnyādervastuno darśanāt "kvaciddeśe" tatsambandhini "prāptyartho" dṛṣṭasyādṛṣṭasya ca "parihārārthaḥ" pravṛttinivṛttilakṣaṇaḥ "sa na syāt" | kiṃ kāraṇam? | "na hi" yasmād "ayaṃ" pratipattā "analaṃ paśyannapi" saṅkīrṇatadadrūpapratibhāsinā pratyakṣeṇa, anyathāsya darśanarūpatāhāneḥ, tathā hi- asaṅkīrṇasyādarśane saṅkīrṇamapi yadi na paśyet tadā loṣṭādiprakhyaṃ kathaṃ kasyacidetaddarśanaṃ syāt? | sa evaṃbhūtaḥ saṅkīrṇadarśanavān pratipattā (

children.text: ) katham "analameva paśyati" na salilādikam? | "kintu" saṅkīrṇarūpavastupratibhāsijñānatayā "salilādikamapi" paśyati | tataḥ kathaṃ "salilārthī tatra" agnimati pradeśe "na pravarteta"? |
children.translated_text: how would he "see only fire" and not water and the like? "Rather," because the cognition appears as an entity of mixed form, he "sees water and the like as well." Therefore, how would "one desiring water not proceed to that" place which contains fire?

body.translated_text: "Granted this happens — what is the fault?" To this he says: "This practical activity (<s>vyavahāra</s>)" known to all people — which, upon seeing some entity such as fire in some place connected with it, has "the purpose of attaining" what has been seen and what has not been seen, and "the purpose of avoiding" — characterized by engagement and withdrawal — "would not exist." What is the reason? "For" — because — "this" cognizer, "even while seeing fire," [sees it] through a direct perception in which the non-own-form is mixed [with the own-form] — for otherwise its character as seeing would be lost. For if, when the unmixed [form] is not seen, even the mixed [form] were not seen, then how would there be anyone's seeing of this [fire], which would appear like a clod of earth? Such a cognizer who possesses mixed seeing,

body.text: parasya vacanāvakāśamāśaṅkayāha- "anupalambhena" ityādi | analapratibhāsinā hi jñānenānalasvarūpameva pratīyate | yastu salilābhāvaḥ sa tatra salilasyānupalambhena | tato jñānadvayena tadatadrūpayorvivekālloke pravṛttinivṛttilakṣaṇaḥ pratiniyato vyavahāraḥ sidhyatīti | siddhāntavādyāha- "ko 'yamanupalambho nāma" iti | kadācit paro brūyāt salilopalambhavirahamātramityata āha- "yadi salila" ityādi | kumārilasya tu salilopalambhanivṛttimātraṃ tuccharūpamabhāvapramāṇatayā nābhimatameva |
body.translated_text: Anticipating an opening for the opponent's statement, he says: "By non-apprehension (<s>anupalambha</s>)" and so forth. For by a cognition in which fire appears, only the own-nature of fire is cognized. But the absence of water there [is known] through the non-apprehension of water. Therefore, through a pair of cognitions, due to the discrimination of the own-form and non-own-form, the determinate practical activity (<s>vyavahāra</s>) characterized by engagement and withdrawal is established in the world — [so the opponent argues]. The proponent says: "What is this so-called non-apprehension (<s>anupalambha</s>)?" Lest the opponent say it is merely the absence of the apprehension of water, he says: "If water (<s>yadi salila</s>)" and so forth. For <s>Kumārila</s>, however, the mere cessation of the apprehension of water, being of a trivial nature, is certainly not accepted as a means of knowledge of absence (<s>abhāvapramāṇa</s>).

children.translated_text: "The non-arising of perception and other [means of knowledge] is called the absence of a means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇābhāva</s>);
or [it is] the non-transformation of the self, or [it is] a cognition directed toward another object."

body.text: iti vacanāt | kintu yo 'sāvātmanaḥ pratiṣedhyavastupratibhāsijñānātmanāpariṇāmaḥ sa tadanyavastupratibhāsijñānasahacarito 'bhyupagantavyo na kevala iti paramabhyupagamayitumasyopanyāsaḥ | tathā cānyavastuvijñānamevābhāvapramāṇamastu, kimapramāṇakasyātmano 'pariṇāmākhyena dharmeṇa parikalpitena? | na ca tadanyavastuvijñānapariṇāmādanya eva tasyāpariṇāmo nāma bhavato 'bhimato bhāvāntarasyaivābhāvatvenopagatatvāt | tulyayogyatārūpasyaikajñānasaṃsargiṇa eva cānyavastuno vijñānaṃ tathopeyaṃ nānyasya, tajjñānāt pratiyogyabhāvasiddheḥ | na hi rūpajñānādrasādyabhāvapratītiryuktimatī deśādiviprakarṣavato vā | anyavastuvijñānaṃ ca pratiniyatarūparpatibhāsyeva | rūpāntarāvabhāsitve hi tasya salilopalambhābhāva eva na sidhyet | evaṃ ca pratiyogyabhāvaḥ pratyakṣāvabhāsita eva | tadabhāvavyavahāre tvasmadabhimataivānupalabdhirāyāteti pratipādayitumasyopanyāsaḥ | tatra yadi salilopalambhābhāvaḥ tuccharūpo 'nupalambhastadā kathamabhāvaḥ (

children.text: ) kasyacit pratipattiḥ pariccheda iti yāvat, paricchedasya jñānadharmatvāt | atha na tasya pratipattirūpateṣyate kintu taddhetubhāva ityata āha- "pratipattiheturvā" iti | nahi sarvasāmarthyavirahalakṣaṇasyābhāvasya pratipattiṃ prati hetubhāvo yuktaḥ | hetubhāve vā tasyānapekṣitasahakāriṇo nityaṃ tajjñānajananādabhāvajñānamevaikaṃ pratipattuḥ syāt, jñānāntarasyāvakāśa eva na bhavet |
children.translated_text: the cognition of anything — i.e., the ascertainment — given that ascertainment is a property of cognition? If, on the other hand, it is not held to have the character of cognition, but rather to be a cause of that [cognition], then he says: "Or [it is] a cause of cognition (<s>pratipattihetuvā</s>)." For it is not reasonable that absence, characterized as the complete lack of all capacity, should be a cause with respect to cognition. Or if it were a cause, then since it requires no auxiliary conditions, it would always generate that cognition, and there would be only the single cognition of absence for the cognizer; there would be no room whatsoever for any other cognition.

body.translated_text: So states [<s>Kumārila</s>]. But the non-transformation of the self, which takes the form of a cognition in which the object to be negated appears — this must be accepted as accompanied by a cognition in which another object appears, not as bare [non-transformation] alone. This passage is introduced in order to bring the opponent to accept this. And thus, let the cognition of another object itself be the means of knowledge of absence — what need is there for the postulated property called "non-transformation of the self," which is not a means of knowledge [on its own]? Nor is this so-called non-transformation of the self, as you conceive it, anything other than the cognition-of-another-object transformation, since [you yourself] accept a positive entity as [constituting] absence. And the cognition of another object must be understood in this way only with respect to another object that shares the same sphere (<s>tulyayogyatā</s>) and is connected with a single cognition, not with respect to any [arbitrary] other — because the absence of the counter-positive is established from the cognition of that [appropriate other]. For the cognition of absence of taste and the like from the cognition of visible form is not reasonable, nor [is it reasonable] in the case of one spatially remote and so forth. And the cognition of another object must appear with a determinate form only. For if it appeared as a different form, the very absence of the apprehension of water would not be established. And thus, the absence of the counter-positive is indeed not manifested in direct perception. But in the practical usage of that absence, it is the <s>anupalabdhi</s> (non-apprehension) as we maintain it that comes into play — this passage is introduced to demonstrate this. In that case, if the absence of the apprehension of water is a trivial non-apprehension, then how is absence

body.text: na cājñātasyāsya nāstitājñānajananaṃ yuktamityāha- "tasyāpi" salilopalambhābhāvasya kathaṃ pratipattiḥ? | athāyaṃ salilopalambhābhāvaḥ svayamapratīta eva salilābhāvapratītiṃ janayati tadā kasyacidapi | tadevāha- "tasya" salilopalambhābhāvasya tato vā salilādanyasyānalādeḥ ‘vijñānaṃ vānyavastuni'; ityata ātmano 'pariṇāmasya pṛthagavasthāpanāt, tatrāpi tadaṅgīkaraṇe cātmano 'pariṇāmasya tadātmakatvānna tato bhedena vyavasthāpyeta | tataśca kasyacidapi tasya tadanyasya vāpratipattāvapi yadyabhāvaḥ salilādeḥ pratīyate tadā svāpādyavasthāsvapi salilādyabhāvaḥ kiṃ na pratīyate? | tadāpi tadabhāvaḥ pratīyetetyetadvicāritam pramāṇaviniścaye, tata evāvadhāraṇīyam | vyavadhānādigrahaṇena caitaddarśayatyanyavastuno 'pyanyatvaṃ tattulyayogyatārūpāpekṣameva, na tadanapekṣamupeyam | tathā cāsmadupavarṇitānupalabdhisiddhiriti | yada caivamuktena prakāreṇānupalambhena salilābhāvapratītirna yujyate 'nalapratibhāsinaśca jñānasya pratiniyatākāratā nābhyupagamyate "tasmādayam" analadarśī pratipattānalaṃ "paśyannapi" saṅkīrṇarūpapratibhāsinā jñānena ‘analo 'yaṃ na salilam'; iti nādhyavasyati anadhyavasyaṃśca salilarūpasyāpi pratibhāsanāt tadarthī "na tiṣṭhet" pravarteta "nāpi pratiṣṭheta" salilārthī na pravarteta | tathāhi- salilaṃ nāma taducyate yat sarvodanyāsantāpādyapanayanakṣamaṃ sakalatadanyarūpāsaṃkīrṇapratiniyatākārajñānāvabhāsi | idaṃ tvanyadeva śabalarūpaṃ kimapyavabhāsata iti | (

children.translated_text: Hbṭ 192
) "And consequently," since engagement and withdrawal, being mutually contradictory, cannot be performed simultaneously, "an insurmountable calamity would befall the apprehender."

body.translated_text: And it is not reasonable that the cognition of the non-existence of something unknown should be produced — thus he says "of that too" — how is there apprehension of this absence of water-perception? Now, if this absence of water-perception, itself unapprehended, generates the cognition of the absence of water, then of anything at all. That is what he states — "of that" absence of water-perception, or from that, i.e., from something other than water such as fire, 'or cognition in another object'; therefore, since one's own non-modification cannot be established separately, and if that is accepted there too, since one's own non-modification is of that nature, it cannot be established as distinct from it. And consequently, even if there is no apprehension of that or of what is other than it, if the absence of water and so forth is cognized, then why is the absence of water and so forth not cognized even in states such as sleep? Whether the absence of that is cognized even then — this has been examined in the <s>Pramāṇaviniścaya</s>, and should be ascertained from there. And by the inclusion of obstruction and similar factors, he shows this: the otherness of another object too is dependent on equal eligibility in the relevant respect, and should not be accepted as independent of that. And thus the establishment of <s>anupalabdhi</s> (non-apprehension) as described by us follows. And when in this manner cognition of the absence of water is not possible through <s>anupalambha</s> (non-apprehension) as stated, and the determinate character of the cognition appearing as fire is not accepted — "therefore this" one who sees fire, the apprehender of fire, "even while seeing" it, through a cognition appearing with a mixed form, does not ascertain 'this is fire, not water'; and not ascertaining thus, since even the form of water appears, "he would not remain" as one desiring fire, nor would he "settle" — he would not proceed as one desiring water. For indeed, what is called water is that which is capable of removing thirst, heat, and so forth of all beings, and which appears in cognition of a determinate character with a form unmixed with all other forms. But this appears as something else entirely, of variegated form. (

body.text: atra parasya vacanāvakāśamāśaṅkayāha- "tata eva" ityādi | na mayā salilopalambhanivṛttimātrāt tu ccharūpāt tadabhāvagatirucyate, yathoktadoṣaprasaṅgāt | kintu yadetadekasya kevalasyānalasya darśanaṃ tata evānyasya tatrāpratibhāsamānasya salilasyābhāvagatirbhavati ‘vijñānaṃ vānyavastuni'; iti vacanāt |
body.translated_text: Here, anticipating an opportunity for the opponent's response, he says "from that very" and so forth. I do not assert that the cognition of its absence arises merely from the cessation of water-perception, i.e., from a bare form, since the stated fault would follow. Rather, it is from this very seeing of one thing alone, namely fire, that there arises the cognition of the absence of water — which does not appear there — as something other than it, on account of the statement 'or cognition in another object.'

body.text: siddhāntavādyāha- "kathamekam" ityādi | kena punaḥ sāmarthyena tadekadarśanam "anyābhāvaṃ pratyāyayati?" | tathāhi- tasmin dṛśyamāne tadevāstītyavagacchatu, tadanyattu nāstīti kimiti pratyetīti | "tasyaiva" paridṛśyamānasyānalādeḥ "kevalasya" salilāsaṃsṛṣṭarūpasya "darśanād" analajñāne pratibhāsanāt ‘salilaṃ nāsti'; iti niścayaḥ sañjāyate | tathāhi- anala iva salilamapi yadi tatrābhaviṣyat tadapyanalavad darśane pratyayabhāsiṣyata tayoḥ svajñānaṃ pratyaviśiṣṭatvād yogyatāyā naikasya pratibhāso yuktaḥ | tasmādekapratibhāsanamanyābhāvanāntarīyakaṃ ityanyābhāve tato jñānamutpadyate anyavastuni ca vijñānaṃ nāstīti jñānaṃ janayati | tathānyad vasut pararūpāsaṃkīrṇasvabhāvatayaiva tathocyate | tadrūpatayaiva ca tajjñānamanyat pratiyadevaṃ vyapadiśyate 'nyathā tadayogādityanyapratipattireva tadabhāvavikalpaheturiti siddhāntavādyāha- "idameva" ityādi | nanvasmābhiridameva prāgabhihitaṃ "tayoḥ satoḥ naikarūpaniyatā pratipattiḥ asambhavāt" ityādibhirvacanaiḥ | tato yadevānyāsaṃsargiṇaḥ kevalasya pratibhāsanaṃ tadeva tadanyābhāvasyāpi, tasyaiva kevalasya tadanyābhāvātmakatvādanyasya cābhāvāṃśasya nirastatvāt | tataḥ pratyakṣāvabhāsitatvāt tadabhāvasya tabdalāt pāścātyaṃ vyavahārapravartanarūpaṃ nāstitājñānaṃ vikalpakamājāyate | (

children.translated_text: Hbṭ 193

children.text: ) na tu tenāpratipannaṃ kiñcidavagamyate, yatastadanyavastuni vijñānaṃ pratyakṣātmakamapyanavagate tadanyābhāve jñānaṃ janayat pṛthagabhāvapramāṇatayā vyavasthāpyeta | tathā hi- tadanyākāraśūnya eva tadekajñānākāraḥ saṃvedyate | tatastatsaṃvedanameva tadabhāvasaṃvedanam | nahi vikalpajñānasyāpi tadākāraśūnyarūpasaṃvedanādanyattadabhāvasaṃvedanaṃ nāma | kevalamasya vikalparūpataivātiricyate | tato yathā nirvikalpajñānāvasite kvacidanale ‘analo 'trāsti'; iti pāścātyo vikalpo vyavahārapravartanamātraṃ na tataḥ pṛthak pramāṇaṃ yathoktaṃ prāk, tathā nāstitājñānamapi vikalpakaṃ tatphaṃladvāreṇa vānyavastuvijñānaṃ na pratyakṣāt pṛthagabhāvākhyaṃ pramāṇamiti | tasmād yadevāsmābhirabhihitaṃ tadanyābhāvapratītiṃ prati, tadeva tvayāpyabhidhīyata iti kasmāt paruṣamivābhāti yatastadanabhyupagamena pṛthagabhāvākhyaṃ pramāṇamabhyupagatamityupahasati | tathā hyagatyedānīṃ tvayocyate na madhyasthatayā anyathedameva kiṃ na pūrvamevābhihitam?, yata ālajālabhidhānenātmā parikleśita ityupasaṃharannāha- " tasmāt tīrādarśineva" ityādi | yathā kila vahanārūḍhairvarṇigbhiḥ śakunirmucyate api nāma tīraṃ drakṣyatīti | sa yadā sarvataḥ paryaṭaṃstīreṃ nāsādayati tadā vahanamevāgacchati tadvadetadapi draṣṭavyam | yataścāvaśyabhyupagamanīyo 'yaṃ pakṣastasmānna kiñcidanayāvidyamānapratiṣṭhānayā diśaḥ pratipattyā prayojanam |
children.translated_text: ) But nothing unapprehended by it is cognized thereby, for if cognition regarding another object, though of the nature of <s>pratyakṣa</s> (direct perception), were to generate cognition of the absence of that other without that absence being apprehended, it would be established as a separate means of valid knowledge called <s>abhāvapramāṇa</s> (absence as a means of knowledge). For consider: the cognitive form of the cognition of that one alone is apprehended as devoid of the form of what is other than it. Therefore, the apprehension of that is itself the apprehension of the absence of that. For even in the case of conceptual cognition, there is no apprehension of the absence of that other than the apprehension of a form devoid of that character. It is only the conceptual nature of this that is additionally present. Therefore, just as the subsequent conceptual construction 'fire exists here' regarding some fire ascertained by <s>nirvikalpajñāna</s> (non-conceptual cognition) is merely the initiation of conventional activity and is not a <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge) separate from it, as was stated before, so too the conceptual cognition of non-existence, or the cognition of another object through the channel of its result, is not a <s>pramāṇa</s> called <s>abhāva</s> (absence) separate from <s>pratyakṣa</s> (direct perception). Therefore, what was stated by us regarding the cognition of the absence of what is other than it — that very thing is being stated by you as well, so why does it appear as if harsh? — since by not accepting that, a separate <s>pramāṇa</s> called <s>abhāva</s> is accepted — thus he mocks. For indeed, now being cornered you say this, not from a neutral standpoint — otherwise why was this very thing not stated earlier? — since by the assertion of a web of fallacies, one has only tormented oneself — thus concluding, he says "therefore, like one who sees the shore" and so forth. Just as, it is said, merchants who have boarded a ship release a bird, thinking 'perhaps it will see the shore.' When, having wandered in all directions, it does not reach the shore, it returns to the ship itself — so too should this be regarded. And since this position must necessarily be accepted, therefore there is no purpose served by this cognition of directions that has no real foundation.

body.translated_text: The <s>siddhāntavādin</s> (proponent of the established view) says "how can one" and so forth. By what capacity does that perception of one thing alone "produce the cognition of the absence of others?" For consider: when that is being perceived, let one understand that just that exists; but why should one cognize that what is other than it does not exist? "From the seeing of that very" thing being perceived, such as fire, "alone," i.e., with a form unmixed with water, "from the appearance" in the fire-cognition, the certainty 'water does not exist' arises. For consider: if water, like fire, had been present there, it too would have appeared in perception just as fire does, since the two are undifferentiated with respect to their capacity to produce their own cognition — the appearance of only one is not reasonable. Therefore, the appearance of one alone necessarily entails the absence of others, and so it generates cognition of absence, i.e., the cognition 'it does not exist,' regarding the absence of others, and it generates cognition, i.e., the cognition 'it does not exist,' regarding other objects. Likewise, another object is called such only by virtue of having a nature unmixed with the form of other things. And it is precisely as having that nature that the cognition of it is designated as cognizing something other — otherwise, since that would be impossible — thus the cognition of something other is itself the cause of the conceptual construction of the absence of that. So the <s>siddhāntavādin</s> says "this very" and so forth. Indeed, this very thing was stated by us previously, through the statements "of those two existing things, there is no apprehension determined to one form alone, because of its impossibility" and so forth. Therefore, that which is the appearance of what is sole, unmixed with others, that itself is also of the absence of what is other than it, since that which is sole is itself of the nature of the absence of what is other than it, and since the aspect of absence of the other is excluded. Therefore, since it is manifested by <s>pratyakṣa</s> (direct perception), the conceptual cognition of non-existence, which takes the form of subsequent conventional activity, arises from the absence of that, i.e., as a result of it. (

body.text: tadevaṃ parasyānyabhāvatadabhāvayorliṅgaliṅgibhāvamicchataḥ sambandhābhāvādasāvayuktaḥ iti pratipādite pareṇa ‘asati sambandhe 'nyabhāvagatyāpi tadabhāvagatirna syāt'; iti codite ‘na vai kutaścit sambandhād'; ityādyabhihitam | ataḥ ‘anyabhāva eva tadabhāvo 'nyabhāvagatireva ca tadabhāvagatiḥ'; iti prasādhayatā kumārilaparikalpitaḥ kasyacidabhāvaniścayārthamabhāvapramāṇavādaḥ prasaṅgato nirastaḥ samprati tu-
body.translated_text: Thus, after it has been demonstrated that the opponent's position — who desires a relation of <s>liṅga</s> (logical mark) and <s>liṅgin</s> (what is marked) between the existence of one thing and the absence of another — is unjustified due to the absence of such a relation, and after the opponent has objected 'in the absence of a relation, even from the cognition of the existence of another thing, there should be no cognition of its absence,' the reply 'not indeed from any relation' and so forth was given. Hence, in establishing that 'the existence of another is itself the absence of that, and the cognition of the existence of another is itself the cognition of the absence of that,' the doctrine of <s>abhāvapramāṇa</s> (absence as a separate means of valid knowledge), devised by <s>Kumārila</s> for the purpose of ascertaining the absence of something, has been incidentally refuted. But now —

body.text: "vastvasaṅkarasiddhiśca tatprāmāṇyasamāśritā"
body.translated_text: "And the establishment of the non-confusion of entities is dependent on the validity of that [i.e., <s>abhāvapramāṇa</s>]."

body.text: ityetadāhatya nirākartuṃ pūrvapakṣamutthāpayannāha- "yadyekaparicchedādevaḥ" ityādi | yadi hi "ekasya" kevalasya paricchedādanyasya "vyavacchedaḥ" pratiṣedhaḥ sidhyati tadā sarvasyā a(syā)nyasyāviśeṣeṇaiva "tatra" deśe yatrāsāvekaḥ paridṛśyate tatrābhāvasiddhirbhavet, na tu viśeṣaparigraheṇa tulyā svajñānajananaṃ prati yogyāvasthā yasya tasyaiveti | tathā hi- asau yathā tulyayogyatārūpapadārthaviviktarūpa upalabhyate, tadekākārapratiniyamāt tajjñānaśca, tathā tadatulyayogyatārūpapadārthaviviktatmako 'pi | tataśca tadviviktākāratayā tadanyābhavasādhane viśeṣābhāvāt pradeśarūpajñānaṃ ghaṭābhavamiva rasādyabhāvamapi sādhayet, na vā ghaṭābhāvamapīti |
body.translated_text: Introducing this and raising the <s>pūrvapakṣa</s> (prima facie objection) in order to refute it, he says "if from the ascertainment of one alone" and so forth. If indeed from the ascertainment "of one" thing alone, the "exclusion," i.e., negation, of another is established, then the establishment of the absence of "all" that is other than it, without distinction, should occur "there," in that place where that one thing is perceived — and not through the specific restriction that only that which has an equal state of eligibility for producing its own cognition is excluded. For consider: just as that thing is perceived as having a form distinct from objects of equal eligibility, and its cognition is determined to that one form alone, so too it is distinct in nature from objects of unequal eligibility. And consequently, since there is no difference in establishing the absence of what is other than it by virtue of having a form distinct from it, the cognition of a place-form should establish the absence of taste and so forth just as it establishes the absence of a pot — or else it should not establish even the absence of a pot.

body.text: kiñca, yadetad ‘upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptasyānupalabdhirabhāvasādhanī'; iti viśeṣaṇamuktaṃ tacca na vaktavyam | kiṃ kāraṇam? yato ye 'pyanupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptāsteṣāmapi tatra deśe tadekākāratayā jñānasya vyavacchedo bhavatyeva | tathā hi- yathopalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptāstadekākāravati jñāne na pratibhāsante tataśca vyavacchidyante tathānupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptā apīti kim ‘upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptasya" ityanena viśeṣaṇeneti | evaṃ pūrvapakṣe vyavasthite yadi tadanyavyavacchedaḥ- tataḥ pṛthakkaraṇamanyatvena vyavasthāpanamabhimataṃ tadabhyupagamyata eva | atha taddeśakālayorabhāvaḥ, tadayuktam, yena hi sāmarthyena tulyayogyatārūpasyopalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptasya cābhāvaṃ sādhayati na tatsāmarthyamatulyayogyatārūpe 'nupalbdhilakṣaṇaprāpte vā sambhavati | ‘tayoḥ satornaikarūpaniyatā pratipattiḥ asambhavāt'; ityevaṃ hi tadabhāvasādhanam | na caitadanyatra sambhavatīti pratipādayitum "ekātmaparicchedāt" ityādinopakramate | yat puro 'vasthitaṃ pratyakṣe 'vabhāsate tasyaikasyātmanaḥ pratiniyatasya rūpasya paricchedāt tadākārotpattyā vidhivikalpotpādanena ca yaḥ "tadanyaḥ" tato 'nyastadvayatiriktastasya sarvasya ya "ātmā" svabhāvastato (

children.translated_text: Hbṭ 195

children.text: ) "vyavacchedo" bhedanaṃ pṛthakkaraṇamanyatvasādhanamasaṅkīrṇarūpatāpratyāyanaṃ bhavati | kathaṃ punarekātmaparicchedādeva tasya tadanyātmano vyavacchedaḥ pratyakṣeṇa kriyate?, yāvatā pratyakṣaṃ puro 'vasthitapadārthasāmarthyabhāvi tadrūpameva pratipadyatām | yattu tadvayatiriktamaśeṣapadārthajātaṃ tadātmanastasya puro 'vasthitasya kathaṃ tavdyavacchedakam? ataḥ tavdyavacchedārthamabhāvapramāṇamabhyupeyam, yato-
children.translated_text: ) "exclusion" — differentiation, separate determination, establishment of otherness, making known the unmixed nature — occurs. But how does the exclusion of the nature of what is other than it occur through <s>pratyakṣa</s> (direct perception) from the ascertainment of the nature of one alone? Since <s>pratyakṣa</s>, arising through the power of the object standing before it, apprehends only its form. But the entire mass of objects other than it — of the nature of that which stands before it — how can that be what excludes it? Therefore, <s>abhāvapramāṇa</s> (absence as a means of valid knowledge) must be accepted for the purpose of that exclusion, since —

body.translated_text: Moreover, the qualification that was stated — 'the non-apprehension of what has met the conditions for apprehension is what establishes absence' — that too should not be stated. For what reason? Because even those that have not met the conditions for apprehension are excluded there, in that place, by virtue of the cognition being of that one form alone. For consider: just as those that have met the conditions for apprehension do not appear in the cognition that has that one form alone and are therefore excluded, so too those that have not met the conditions for apprehension — so what is the purpose of the qualification "of what has met the conditions for apprehension"? When the <s>pūrvapakṣa</s> (prima facie position) is thus established: if the exclusion of what is other than it — then if what is intended is the separate determination, i.e., the establishment as other, that is conceded indeed. But if what is meant is the absence in that place and time, that is unjustified, because the capacity by which it establishes the absence of what has equal eligibility in form and what has met the conditions for apprehension — that capacity is not possible with respect to what is unequal in eligibility of form or what has not met the conditions for apprehension. For it has been stated that the establishment of the absence of that is through the principle 'of those two existing things, there is no apprehension determined to one form alone, because of its impossibility.' And since this does not obtain elsewhere, he begins with "from the ascertainment of the nature of one alone" and so forth. From the ascertainment of the nature of that one alone — of the determinate form of that which stands before one and appears in <s>pratyakṣa</s> (direct perception) — through the arising of that cognitive form and through the production of a positive conceptual construction, the "exclusion" of what is "other than that," i.e., of everything other than and distinct from it — the differentiation, the separate determination, the establishment of otherness, the making known of an unmixed nature — occurs. But how does the exclusion of the nature of what is other than it occur through <s>pratyakṣa</s> (direct perception) from the ascertainment of the nature of one alone? After all, <s>pratyakṣa</s>, arising through the power of the object standing before it, may apprehend only its form. But the entire mass of objects other than it — how can that be what excludes it from the nature of what stands before it? Therefore, <s>abhāvapramāṇa</s> (absence as a means of valid knowledge) must be accepted for the purpose of that exclusion, since —

body.text: "vastvasaṃkarasiddhiśca tatprāmāṇyasamāśritā" iti |
body.translated_text: "And the establishment of the non-confusion of entities is dependent on the validity of that [i.e., <s>abhāvapramāṇa</s>]."

body.text: ata āha- "tadātmaniyatapratibhāsajñānād" iti | yataḥ puro 'vasthitasyaikasya vastunaḥ pararūpāsaṃkīrṇa ātmā, sarvabhāvānāṃ svabhāvata eva svasvabhāvavyavasthiteḥ pararūpeṇāsaṃkīrṇasvabhāvatvāt | anyathā kathamabhāvapramāṇato 'pyasāṃkaryameṣāṃ sidhyet? | saṃkīrṇarūpāṇāmasāṅkaryasādhane tasya bhrāntatāprasaṅgāt | tasmin pararūpāsaṃkīrṇe svabhāvata eva tadātmaniyato yaḥ pratibhāsaḥ pararūpapratibhāsāsaṃkīrṇaḥ tadekapadārthasāmarthyabhāvini pratyakṣe pararūpapratibhāsāyogāt tasya bhrāntatāpattyā pratyakṣātāhāneḥ | taduktam- "taddhayarthasamarthyenotpadyamānaṃ tadrūpamevānukuryāt" iti | tasya tadātmaniyatapratibhāsaya jñānāt pratyakṣeṇa svasaṃvittyā saṃvedanāt | tatsaṃvedanameva hi pratyakṣasyātadrūpād "vyavacchedanaṃ" pṛthakkaraṇaṃ tabdalenaiva ca pāścātyaḥ ‘anyātmakametanna bhavati'; ityasāṃkaryavasthāpratyayo vikalpakaḥ saṃjāyate gṝhītagrāhī | na tenāpūrvaṃ kiñcit pratīyate, pararūpāsaṃkīrṇasyātmanaḥ pratyakṣeṇaiva tadākārānukāriṇā paricchedāditi |
body.translated_text: Therefore he says "from a cognition whose appearance is determined to the nature of that" and so forth. Since the nature of one object standing before one is unmixed with the form of others — because all entities are by their very nature established in their own respective natures, and hence have a nature unmixed with the form of others. Otherwise, how could the non-confusion of these be established even through <s>abhāvapramāṇa</s> (absence as a means of valid knowledge)? Since in establishing the non-confusion of things whose forms are confused, that [<s>abhāvapramāṇa</s>] would turn out to be erroneous. In that which is by its very nature unmixed with the form of others, the appearance that is determined to its own nature, unmixed with the appearance of other forms — since in <s>pratyakṣa</s> (direct perception), which arises through the power of that one object alone, the appearance of other forms is impossible, and otherwise the status of <s>pratyakṣa</s> would be lost through the consequence of its being erroneous. As was stated: "for that, arising through the power of the object, would reproduce only that form." From that cognition whose appearance is determined to its own nature — through <s>pratyakṣa</s>, through <s>svasaṃvitti</s> (self-awareness), through apprehension. That apprehension itself is the "exclusion" from what is not of that nature, the differentiation from <s>pratyakṣa</s>, and as a result of that very thing, the subsequent conceptual cognition 'this is not of the nature of that other' — a conceptual construction establishing the state of non-confusion — arises, grasping what has already been grasped. Nothing new is cognized by it, since the nature that is unmixed with the form of others has already been ascertained by <s>pratyakṣa</s> itself, which reproduces that very cognitive form.

body.text: yadi nāma tadātmaniyatapratibhāsajñānaṃ tathāpi kathamanyātmanaḥ tasya pṛthakkaraṇam? ityata āha- "na hi tadātma" ityādi | yasmāttasya vastuno ya ātmā pararūpāsaṃkīrṇaḥ sa tadanyasya śeṣasya vastuna ātmā na bhavati, sarvasya tato 'nyasvabhāvatvāt, anyathā tadanyatvahāneriti | tasmāttadātmaniyatapratibhāsajñānameva (

children.translated_text: Hbṭ 196

children.text: ) tadanyebhyo nivartanam | nahi jñānenārtho haste gṛhītvānyato nivartanīyaḥ | kevalamanyarūpāsaṃkīrṇasyaikasyātmano 'nukaraṇamevāsyānyato nivartanamucyata iti | athānyātmānaḥ svaviṣayaṃ na nivartayet, tadāsya viṣayasyānyātmanaḥ sakāśādavyavacchede pṛthagavyavasthāpane parātmano 'pi tatra paricchedaḥ syāt, anyathā tadaparicchedasyaivaikātmaparicchedātmanastannivartanarūpatā syāt | tataścāvyavacchede 'nyātmanastatparicchedaprasaṅgāt pravṛttinivṛttyorabhāva iti pūrvaḥ prasaṅgo ‘na hyayamanalaṃ paśyannapi'; ityādikaḥ |
children.translated_text: ) the withdrawal from what is other than it. For it is not the case that cognition must grasp an object by hand and withdraw it from another. Rather, the reproduction of the nature of one thing alone, which is unmixed with the form of others, is itself called its withdrawal from others. Now, if the nature of what is other did not withdraw its own object, then since its object would not be excluded from, i.e., separately established from, the nature of what is other, there would be apprehension of the nature of the other there as well; otherwise, the very non-apprehension of that would be of the nature of the ascertainment of the nature of one alone, which would itself be of the nature of withdrawal from it. And consequently, in the case of non-exclusion, since there would be the consequence of apprehending the nature of what is other than it, there would be the absence of both engagement and withdrawal — thus the earlier <s>prasaṅga</s> (absurd consequence) beginning with 'for this one, even while seeing fire' and so forth.

body.translated_text: Even if the cognition has an appearance determined to the nature of that, still how is the differentiation of the nature of what is other than it achieved? To this he says "for the nature of that is not" and so forth. Since the nature of that object, which is unmixed with the form of others, is not the nature of the remaining objects other than it, because everything is of a nature different from it — otherwise, the otherness from it would be lost. Therefore, the cognition whose appearance is determined to the nature of that alone is itself (

body.text: na kevalamanyātmanastannivartayati tadātmano 'pyaśeṣamanyaditi darśayannāha- "taṃ ca" agrataḥ sthitaṃ deśakālasvabhāvāvasthāniyataṃ tadanyadeśādibhyo vyāvṛttātmanaḥ svahetubhyaḥ evāsya bhāvāt, "tadātmanā" deśādiniyatenātmanā tathāvidhasvabhāvasyaivānukārādupalabhamānā buddhiḥ "tathātvapracyutim" anyadeśakālasvabhāvāvasthatām "asya" svaviṣayasya "vyavacchinatti" tataḥ pṛthakkaroti | kasmātpunaranyadeśāditāṃ tataḥ pṛthagavasthāpayati ityata āha- "evaṃ hi" yasmādanyadeśatādestataḥ pṛthakkaraṇe sati taddeśādiniyataḥ padārthaḥ paricchinno bhavati, tadrūpasyaivānukārād | yadyanyathābhāvo 'nyadeśāditā tadrūpānanukārāvdyavacchinnaḥ- bhavati tathātvaṃ ca taddeśādiniyatatvaṃ ca, tadā tasyaiva dṛśyamānasya bhavati nānyasyānyadeśādimataḥ | yata evam "iti" tasmādanyathābhūtādanyadeśādimatastathābhūtaṃ taddeśādimaṃtaṃ "vyavacchindatyeva" nivartayantyeva tat paricchinattīti pūrvakasyopasaṃhāraḥ | tathā "tathābhūtādanyathābhūtaṃ vyavacchindatyeva" iti dvitīyasyopasaṃhāraḥ kārya iti | "evam" uktena nyāyena "ekasya" pramāṇasya pratyakṣasyānumānasya vā tasyāpyevameva svaviṣayaparicchedād "vṛttiḥ" pravṛttiḥ sarvabhāvān "dvairāśye" tattve 'nyatve ca "vyavasthāpayati" | tatastatparicchedakapramāṇabalenaivāsāṅkaryasiddhiḥ | kiṃ tadarthikayāpyabhāvakalpanayeti? |
body.translated_text: Not only does it exclude what is of a different nature from that, but it also shows that even what is of that nature [excludes] everything else — thus he says "that" (<s>taṃ ca</s>). The object standing before [cognition], determined by a fixed spatial-temporal-essential state, exists only from its own causes as having a nature distinguished from other locations and so forth. "By that nature" (<s>tadātmanā</s>) — cognition, apprehending [the object] through the reproduction of only such a nature determined by location and so forth, "discriminates the deviation from such-ness" (<s>tathātvapracyutim</s>) — that is, the state of having other location, time, essential nature, and condition — "of this" (<s>asya</s>), its own object, separating it therefrom. Why then does it separate the state of being in another location and so forth from that? To this he says "for thus" (<s>evaṃ hi</s>) — because when separation from the state of being in another location and so forth is accomplished, the entity determined by that [particular] location and so forth becomes delimited, since only its own form is reproduced. If the state of being otherwise — the state of having other location and so forth — were not discriminated due to non-reproduction of that form, then both the such-ness and the determination by that location and so forth [would be lost], and it would belong to that very thing seen, not to another possessing other location and so forth. Since this is so, "therefore" (<s>iti</s>) — it "indeed discriminates" (<s>vyavacchindatyeva</s>) the thing determined by that location and so forth from what is otherwise constituted, possessing other location and so forth — by excluding it, it delimits it. This is the conclusion of the first [point]. Likewise, "it indeed discriminates what is otherwise constituted from what is so constituted" — this conclusion of the second [point] should be understood. "Thus" (<s>evam</s>), by the method stated, the "operation" (<s>vṛttiḥ</s>), i.e., the functioning, "of a single" <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid cognition) — whether <s>pratyakṣa</s> (direct perception) or <s>anumāna</s> (inference), which likewise delimits its own object — "establishes" (<s>vyavasthāpayati</s>) all entities "in the twofold classification" (<s>dvairāśye</s>), namely <s>tattva</s> (identity) and <s>anyatva</s> (otherness). Therefore, the establishment of non-confusion (<s>asāṅkarya</s>) is accomplished by the very force of the <s>pramāṇa</s> that delimits it. What need is there for the postulation of a [separate] absence cognition for that purpose?

body.text: nanu ca vikalpavyāpāra eṣa ‘idamanyātmakaṃ na bhavati anyathaitadātmakam'; iti | pratyakṣaṃ ca nirvikalpakamiṣyate tat kathamasāṃkaryasiddhistataḥ? ityata āha- "tasyānvaye" tyādi | taddhi pratyakṣaṃ vidhipratiṣedhavikalpau yadā svaviṣaye janayati tadaivāsya sāphalyam, tadaiva ca pramāṇamiṣyate nānyadā ata evaikasyārthasvabhāvasyāpratipannāṃśābhāvāt sarvātmanā paricchede 'pi bhrāntikāraṇasadbhāvāt kṣaṇikatādāvanvayavyatirekabuddhī janayitumasāmarthyāt tatrāsya prāmāṇyaṃ neṣyata iti |
body.translated_text: But [the opponent says]: this is the operation of <s>vikalpa</s> (conceptual cognition) — 'this is not of the nature of another, otherwise it would be of that nature.' And <s>pratyakṣa</s> (direct perception) is accepted as <s>nirvikalpaka</s> (non-conceptual). So how can the establishment of non-confusion (<s>asāṅkarya</s>) come from that? To this he says "in its presence" (<s>tasyānvaye</s>) and so forth. For that <s>pratyakṣa</s> achieves its purpose only when it generates <s>vidhivikalpa</s> (positive conceptual cognition) and <s>pratiṣedhavikalpa</s> (negative conceptual cognition) regarding its own object, and only then is it accepted as a <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid cognition), not otherwise. For this very reason — since there is no unapprehended aspect of a single object-nature, even though there is complete delimitation, because there exist causes of error, and because [perception alone] is incapable of generating cognitions of invariable concomitance and exclusion (<s>anvayavyatirekabuddhī</s>) regarding momentariness and such [properties] — its authority as a <s>pramāṇa</s> is not accepted in those cases.

body.text: syānmatam- dvairāśyasādhane 'pyasāṃkaryasiddhyarthā mā bhūdabhāvapramāṇakalpanā kintu prakārāntarābhāvasiddhyarthā bhaviṣyati | na hi tadabhāvasiddhau pratyakṣasya kaścid vyāpāraḥ pratipādita iti ata āha "tadvyatirikte"tyādi | tasmāt paridṛśyamānād vyatiriktasyāśeṣasya vastuno vyavacchedena tataḥ pṛthakkaraṇenānyatvena yā vyāptistatsādhanādeva prakārāntarasya tattvānyatvabahirbhūtasyābhāvaḥ sidhyati | tatastadarthamapi nābhāvapramāṇakalpanā yukteti |
body.translated_text: One might think: even if there is no need to postulate an absence-<s>pramāṇa</s> for the purpose of establishing non-confusion through the twofold classification, there will be [need for it] for the purpose of establishing the absence of a third category. For no operation of <s>pratyakṣa</s> (direct perception) has been demonstrated in establishing that absence. To this he says "in what is different from that" (<s>tadvyatirikte</s>) and so forth. The absence of a third category — one outside <s>tattva</s> (identity) and <s>anyatva</s> (otherness) — is established by the very proof of the <s>vyāpti</s> (pervasion) that consists in the exclusion, i.e., the separation and otherness, of everything that is different from what is directly observed. Therefore, the postulation of an absence-<s>pramāṇa</s> is not justified even for that purpose.

body.text: atha matam- sarvasyāparidṛṣṭasya dṛśyamānādanyatayā vyāptiṃ naivaṃ pratyakṣaṃ sādhayati tat kutastṛtīyarāśyabhāvaḥ pratyakṣata eva syāt, yato 'bhāvaprāmāṇyakalpanā vyarthā bhavedityata āha- "tasya" tṛtīyarāśitayā kalpyamānasya tato dṛṣṭādanyatayā vyāptyabhāve "tena" pratyakṣeṇa "tato"'rthāt svaviṣayasya "avyavacchedā" dapṛthakkaraṇāt, tadarthasya ca rāśyantaratvena kalpyamānasya svaviṣayādavyavacchedāt apṛthakkaraṇāt punarapi bhāvasya svaviṣayasyāparicchedaprasaṅgāt | sa hi tadviṣayaḥ sakalapararūpāsaṃkīrṇātmā yadi tenātmanā na paricchinnaḥ kathaṃ tena tasya paricchedaḥ? | tenātmanā paricchede vā kathaṃ sarvasya tadanyatayā vyāptyasādhanam? anyathaikasyāpi tadanyatvaṃ na syāt, nimittasya samānatvāditi | yata evaṃ "tasmāt" kvacidvastuni pramāṇaṃ pratyakṣādikaṃ (

children.translated_text: Hbṭ 198

children.text: ) pravṛttaṃ tadvastu pratiniyatenātmanā paricchinatti, tato 'nyattadrūpavikalaṃ vyavacchinatti, tadanyatvena vyavasthāpanāt | tṛtīyasya ca tattvānyatvabahirbhūtasya prakārasyābhāvaṃ sūcayati, sarvasyānyatayā vyāptisādhanāt, tadviruddhasya vā sarvavastuno dvaividhyasya sādhanāditi |
children.translated_text: it delimits that object as having a specifically determined nature, and it discriminates what is other than that as lacking that form, by establishing its otherness from that. And it indicates the absence of a third category outside <s>tattva</s> (identity) and <s>anyatva</s> (otherness), because it establishes the pervasion of everything by otherness, or because it establishes the twofold nature of all entities, which is contradictory to [a third category].

body.translated_text: Now one might think: <s>pratyakṣa</s> (direct perception) does not in this way establish the pervasion of everything unobserved as being other than what is observed. So how could the absence of a third category be [established] from <s>pratyakṣa</s> alone, such that the postulation of the authority of absence [as a separate <s>pramāṇa</s>] would be pointless? To this he says: "of that" (<s>tasya</s>) — if there is no pervasion by otherness from the observed of what is postulated as a third category, then "by that" (<s>tena</s>), i.e., by <s>pratyakṣa</s>, there would be "non-discrimination" (<s>avyavaccheda</s>), i.e., non-separation, of its own object from that, and since what is postulated as belonging to another category would not be separated from its own object, there would again be the absurd consequence of non-delimitation of the object itself. For if that object, whose nature is unmixed with all other forms, is not delimited as having that nature, how can there be delimitation of it by that [cognition]? And if it is delimited as having that nature, how can there be failure to establish the pervasion of everything as other than it? Otherwise, not even a single thing would have otherness from it, since the logical ground would be the same. Since this is so, "therefore" (<s>tasmāt</s>), when a <s>pramāṇa</s> such as <s>pratyakṣa</s> operates upon some object,

body.text: evamekasya pramāṇasya vyāpāra eṣo 'nantarokta iti tamevopasaṃhṛtya sukhapratipattaye darśayannāha- "tathāhi" kvacidvastuni "pramāṇaṃ" pratyakṣādi pravṛttaṃ "tadeva" vastu tadanyasmāt "pārūpād vyavacchinatti" tataḥ pṛthakkaroti tadasaṃkīrṇarūpatayā pratipadyate, paramārthatastasya tadrūpatvāt yathāvastu ca pratyakṣeṇa rūpānukārāt | kimiti pararūpāvdyavacchinatti? | tasyaiva pararūpavikalasyaikarūpasya paricchedāt | tathā "tadanyadeva ca" tasmād dṛśyamānādanyadeva ca vyavacchinatti | kutaḥ? | "tasmāt" svaviṣayāt | na kevalaṃ svaviṣayaṃ parato vyavacchinatti, paramapi svaviṣayād iti | kuta etad? | anyasya pararūpasya tatra khālambane 'paricchedādavaśyamevāparicchinnasya paricchinnādanyatvaṃ bhavati | yata evamataḥ "tad" eva pramāṇamekavastuparicchedakaṃ prakārāntarābhāvaṃ sādhayati, nābhāvākhyam | kuta etat? | tasmiṃ dṛśyamāne vastuni dṛṣṭatadanyatvena tasyānyasya tatrāparicchidyamānasyānyatvaṃ tadanyatvaṃ dṛṣṭāt tadanyatvaṃ "dṛṣṭatadanyatvaṃ" tena sarvasya tavdyatiriktasya vyavasthāpanānna a(panena a) tadanyasyaiva ca yadanyanna bhavati puro 'vasthitaṃ sakalaparabhāvavyāvṛttaṃ tasyaiva tattvena dṛśyamānaprakāratayā vyavasthāpanāditi |
body.translated_text: Thus, the operation of a single <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid cognition) has been described just above. Summarizing that very point and presenting it for easy comprehension, he says "for thus" (<s>tathāhi</s>): a <s>pramāṇa</s> such as <s>pratyakṣa</s> (direct perception), operating upon some object, "discriminates that very" (<s>tadeva</s>) object "from other forms" (<s>pārūpāt</s>), separates it therefrom, and apprehends it as having an unmixed form — because in reality it has that form, and because <s>pratyakṣa</s> reproduces the form as it really is. Why does it discriminate from other forms? Because it delimits it as having a single form, lacking other forms. Likewise, "what is other than that too" (<s>tadanyadeva ca</s>) — it also discriminates what is other than that which is observed. From where? "From that" (<s>tasmāt</s>) — from its own object. Not only does it discriminate its own object from others, but also others from its own object. How so? Because there is no delimitation of what is other — having a different form — in that cognition's object, and necessarily what is not delimited has otherness from what is delimited. Since this is so, "that" (<s>tad</s>) very <s>pramāṇa</s>, which delimits a single object, establishes the absence of a third category — not [a separate <s>pramāṇa</s>] called absence. How so? Because the otherness from the observed — "observed-otherness" (<s>dṛṣṭatadanyatva</s>) — of what is not delimited therein, in that observed object, being other than it, establishes everything different from it in this way; and because what is not other than it, [namely] the object standing before [cognition], distinguished from all other entities, is established as having precisely that identity, as a mode of appearance of the observed.

body.text: amumeva nyāyamanyatrāpyatidiśannāha- "etena kramākramādayaḥ" ityādi | etena anantaroktena nyāyena pratiniyataikapadārtharūpānukāriṇī buddhirupajāyamānā tadviparītarūpaṃ sarvaṃ svaviṣayād vyavacchindatī dvairāśyaṃ tṛtīyaprakārābhāvaṃ ca sādhayatīti ye kecidanyonyavyacchedarūpāḥ kramākramanityānityādayaḥ te vyākhyātāḥ | (

children.translated_text: Hbṭ 199

children.text: ) tathā hi- kāryasya kramamananyasahāyatāṃ pratiyatyeva buddhistasyākramaṃ kāryāntarasāhityaṃ tataḥ pṛthakkaroti | tataḥ kramākramatayā dvaitasiddheḥ tṛtīyasya prakārasya sambhavo nirasto bhavati | kramabhāvavyatirekiṇaḥ sarvasya kāryajanmanaḥ tadanyatayā dvitīyaprakāratayāvasthānāt | evamudayānantaradhvaṃsitā kṣaṇikatocyate iti pratīyatī vyavasthāpanākāla eva buddhistadviparītarūpatāyāḥ svaviṣayādapākaraṇāt tato 'nyatvena prakārāntare 'vasthāpanād rāśyantarābhāva iti |
children.translated_text: For instance: cognition, apprehending the sequence of an effect — its non-simultaneity [with its cause] — separates from it the simultaneity, i.e., the co-occurrence with another effect. Therefore, since the duality of sequence and simultaneity is established, the possibility of a third category is eliminated — because everything in the production of effects that is different from sequential existence is established as belonging to the second category, namely otherness. Similarly, what is called <s>kṣaṇikatā</s> (momentariness) — destruction immediately after arising — is understood [through the same principle]: at the very time of establishing [it], cognition removes the form of its contrary from its own object and establishes it as belonging to another category through otherness, hence the absence of a further category.

body.translated_text: Extending this very principle to other cases as well, he says "thereby sequence and simultaneity and so forth" (<s>etena kramākramādayaḥ</s>) and so forth. By this principle just stated — cognition arising as a reproduction of the form of a single specifically determined entity discriminates everything of contrary form from its own object, and thereby establishes the twofold classification and the absence of a third category — whatever [pairs] have the nature of mutual exclusion, such as sequence and simultaneity (<s>kramākrama</s>), permanent and impermanent (<s>nityānitya</s>), and so forth, are [all] explained.

body.text: tadevamekapramāṇanibandhanāmasāṅkaryasiddhiṃ pratipādyopasaṃharannāha- "tadevam" uktena nyāyena "ekasya" pratiniyatātmana upalambhāt tasyopalabhyamānasya yastato 'nyastattulyayogyatārūpastavdiparīto vā tadrūpavikalastadātmano "vyavacchedaḥ" pṛthakkaraṇaṃ tasyopalabhyamānasyānupalabhyamānasvabhāvād rūpāntareṇa pratibhāsanāt | tathā tasya svaviṣayasya tadanyātmatāyā bhāvapradhānatvānnirddeśasya "vyavacchedo bhavati" asāṅkaryaṃ sidhyati |
body.translated_text: Having thus demonstrated the establishment of non-confusion (<s>asāṅkarya</s>) as grounded in a single <s>pramāṇa</s>, he concludes by saying "thus" (<s>tadevam</s>): by the method stated, from the apprehension of a single [entity] having a specifically determined nature, the "discrimination" (<s>vyavaccheda</s>), i.e., the separation, of what is other than that which is apprehended — whether it has a form of equal fitness or a form contrary to it, i.e., lacking that form — [occurs] because what is apprehended appears with a nature different from what is not apprehended. Likewise, the "discrimination of that" (<s>vyavacchedo bhavati</s>), i.e., non-confusion (<s>asāṅkarya</s>), is established — since the statement is made with emphasis on the positive existence of the otherness of its own object.

body.text: tad yadyetadaviśeṣeṇānyasya sarvasya tannābhāvasiddhiḥ syādityatrābhimataṃ tadā siddhasādhanam, yataḥ sarvamaviśeṣeṇaiva tadekākārayā budhyā tadrūpavikalaṃ svaviṣayādavacchidyate, sarvasyānyarūpasya tatrāpratibhāsanāt | atha taddeśakālayorabhāvaḥ sarvasya tadviparītarūpasya vyavacchedo 'bhimataḥ sa na yukta iti darśayati- "na taddeśakālayoḥ" yatrāsau pratiniyatātmā sakalatrailokyavilakṣaṇaḥ padārtha upalabhyate tatra sarvasyānyasya bhāvasya tattulyayogyatārūpasyetarasya vā vyavacchedaḥ pratiṣedhaḥ | yena hi kāraṇena tattulyayogyatārūpasya tatrāpratibhāsamānasya pratiṣedhastasmin sati tadekarūpaniyatāyāḥ pratipatterasaṃbhavāt tadabhāvanāntarīyikā sā bhāvantī tatpratiṣedhaṃ gamayatīti tatkāraṇamanupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpte tadatulyayogyatārūpe ca na sambhavatīti kathaṃ tadabhāvaḥ sidhyet |
body.translated_text: Now, if the intended [objection] is that this indiscriminate [exclusion] of everything else would not establish absence — that is already established (<s>siddhasādhana</s>), because everything without distinction is discriminated from [the cognition's] own object by that cognition of a single form as lacking that form, since no other form appears therein. But if what is intended is the absence of everything of contrary form at that [particular] place and time — that the discrimination of everything of contrary form [at that location and time] is what is meant — he shows that this is not valid: "not at that place and time" (<s>na taddeśakālayoḥ</s>). The negation of everything else — whether having a form of equal fitness or otherwise — at the place where that entity of specifically determined nature, distinct from the entire triple world, is apprehended [does not follow]. For the reason by which one negates what has a form of equal fitness that does not appear there — since in the presence of that [negation], a cognition determined to that single form would be impossible, and the cognition that necessarily implies its absence conveys its negation — that reason, which amounts to non-apprehension of what is fit to be apprehended (<s>anupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta</s>), does not obtain for what does not have a form of equal fitness, so how could its absence be established?

body.text: etadevopasaṃharannāha- "tasmādatadātmā" ca sarvastadviparītarūpastadekākārayā buddhyā prasādhitaḥ syāt "taddeśakālaśca" tasya pratibhāsamānasya yau deśakālau tau yasya, sa ca syāt | kiṃvat? | rasarūpādivaditi | nahi rūpapratibhāsinā jñānena tadrūpavikalasya rasasya svaviṣayāt pṛthakkaraṇe 'pi tadasāṃkaryasādhane 'pi taddeśakālayorabhāvaḥ sidhyati | tataśca kathaṃ sarvasyātulyayogyāvasthāsyāpi tatrābhāvaḥ syāt?, upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptasyeti viśeṣaṇaṃ vā nocyeta | yata evaṃ "tasmāt" kvacit kadācit kasyacidabhāvasiddhiryathoktādevānupalambhād upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptasya tattulyayogyatārūpopalambhātmanaścetyevaṃrūpāt, na tu sāmānyena yathāhuḥ pare-
body.translated_text: Concluding this very point, he says "therefore what is not of that nature" (<s>tasmādatadātmā</s>): everything of contrary form would be established by that cognition of a single form, "and [what is] at that place and time" (<s>taddeśakālaśca</s>) — what shares the place and time of that which appears — would also [have to be established]. Like what? Like <s>rasa</s> (taste), <s>rūpa</s> (form/color), and so forth. For a cognition that manifests [visual] form, even though it separates taste — which lacks that form — from its own object, and even though it establishes non-confusion with it, does not establish the absence [of taste] at that place and time. Therefore, how could the absence of everything that does not have equal fitness also be [established] there? Or else the qualification "of what is fit to be apprehended" (<s>upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptasya</s>) would not need to be stated. Since this is so, "therefore" (<s>tasmāt</s>), the establishment of absence of something, somewhere, at some time, is only as has been described — from non-apprehension (<s>anupalambha</s>) of what is fit to be apprehended and of the form of apprehension of what has equal fitness — and not in a general way, as others assert:

body.text:
"pramāṇapañcakaṃ yatra vasturūpe na jāyate |
vastusattāvabodhārthaṃ tatrābhāvapramāṇatā ||" iti |
body.translated_text: "Where the fivefold <s>pramāṇa</s> does not arise regarding the nature of an entity, there the authority of absence as a <s>pramāṇa</s> serves to cognize the existence of the entity."

body.text: na hyanupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpte pramāṇapañcakāpravṛttāvapi tadabhāvaḥ sidhyati, satyapi tasmin svabhāvādiviprakarṣeṇa pramāṇapañcakāpravṛttisambhavāditi |
body.translated_text: For even when the fivefold <s>pramāṇa</s> does not operate regarding what is fit to be apprehended, its absence is not established, since it is possible that the fivefold <s>pramāṇa</s> does not operate even when [the object] exists, due to remoteness in essential nature and so forth.

body.text: tadevaṃ prāsaṅgikaṃ parisamāpayya yaduktaṃ pareṇa ‘sa evānyabhāvastadviṣayā copalabdhiḥ tadabhāvasya kiṃ na sādhanam'; iti tatrānyabhāvasya tadabhāvaṃ prati liṅgatve niraste tadviṣayāyā upalabdhernirākurvannāha- "anyābhāvaviṣaye"tyādi | yatpunaruktam- ‘anyabhāvaviṣayopalabdhistadabhāvasya kinna sādhanam'; iti sā tadabhāvasya sādhikeṣṭaivāsmākam, na tu liṅgatvena yathoktavānasi | kiṃ kāraṇam? | yataḥ tatrāpyanyabhāvaviṣayāyāmupalabdhāva'bhāvasya pṛthaganyabhāvāt sādhyatve kalpyamāne sambandhābhāvasya tadabhāvena tulyatvāt | na hi tasyā api anyabhāvarūpāyāḥ tadabhāvena kaścidekārthasamavāyādirūpaḥ sambandho 'stīti |
body.translated_text: Having thus concluded the incidental discussion, regarding what the opponent said — 'the existence of another thing and the cognition directed at it: why is that not the proof of its [i.e., the first thing's] absence?' — after the [possibility of] the other thing's existence being a logical mark (<s>liṅga</s>) for that absence has been refuted, he now refutes the cognition directed at it, saying "regarding the object of another's absence" (<s>anyābhāvaviṣaye</s>) and so forth. As for what was further said — 'why is the cognition directed at the object of another's existence not the proof of that absence?' — that cognition is indeed accepted by us as establishing that absence, but not as a logical mark (<s>liṅga</s>) in the way you have stated. What is the reason? Because even in the case of cognition directed at the object of another's existence, if the absence is postulated as something to be proven separately from the other's existence, then the absence of a connection [between them] is on par with that [very] absence [to be proven]. For there is no connection of the form of co-occurrence in a single locus (<s>ekārthasamavāya</s>) or the like between that cognition — which has the form of the other's existence — and that absence.

body.text: apṛthaksiddherityasyāpi tulyatāṃ darśayannāha- "liṅgāvirbhāve" tyādi | yeyamanyabhāvaviṣayā upalabdhirlliṅgatayocyate tasyāstadviviktapradeśākārāyā (

children.translated_text: Hbṭ 201

children.text: ) "avirbhāvakāla eva" janmakāle pratītikāla eva vā tadabhāvasiddheśca | tathā hi- tatpratibhāsaviviktānyabhāvapratibhāsabuddhisaṃvedanameva tadabhāvasaṃvedanamiti | tadeva sādhayati- na hyanyasya tadviviktasya bhāvaṃ pratipadya pratipattā punaruttarakālaṃ tatpratipatteranyabhāvapratipattestadabhāvenānvayavyatirekau prasādhya pratibandhasādhakena pramāṇena tadabhāvaṃ pratipadyate | kiṃ tarhi? | tadanyaṃ tadviviktarūpaṃ pratipadyamāna eva tasya pratiyogino 'bhāvaṃ pratipadyate, tasyaiva tadabhāvātmakatvāt | tathā hi- saghaṭapradeśāsaṃkīrṇarūpasya kevalapradeśasya darśanameva ghaṭābhāvadarśanam | nahi ‘ghaṭo 'tra nāsti'; ‘ghaṭavānayaṃ na bhavati'; ‘saghaṭādanyaḥ'; ityarthabhedaḥ kaścit | tataḥ saghaṭādanyatayā kevalapradeśasya darśanameva ghaṭābhāvadarśanamiti | ‘ghaṭo 'tra nāstī'; ti jñānaṃ gṛhītagrāhitayā smṛtireveti | kathaṃ jñāyate iti cet | darśanānantaramanvayavyatirekasādhanalakṣaṇena vyavadhānena vinā ‘idaṃ ghaṭaviviktaṃ pradeśavastvasti'; ‘idaṃ tu ghaṭavastu nāsti'; iti pāścātyena vikalpadvayena vyavasthāpanāt | tato nānvayavyatirekānusaraṇamatrāstīti |
children.translated_text: ) "At the very time of manifestation" — at the time of birth, or at the very time of cognition — because the absence of that is established [at that very time]. For thus: the self-awareness of a cognition whose appearance is of another entity, distinct from the appearance of that [negated object], is itself the awareness of the absence of that. He establishes just this: For it is not the case that the cognizer, having cognized the existence of another that is distinct from that [negated object], subsequently at a later time establishes <s>anvaya</s> (positive concomitance) and <s>vyatireka</s> (negative concomitance) through the absence of that from the cognition of another entity and the cognition of that [negated object], and then cognizes the absence of that through a <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid cognition) that establishes the necessary connection. Rather, in the very act of cognizing something other — something whose form is distinct from that [negated object] — one cognizes the absence of the counter-positive, because that [cognition of something other] itself has the nature of the absence of that. For thus: the seeing of a bare location whose form is unmixed with a pot-possessing location is itself the seeing of the absence of a pot. For there is no difference in meaning whatsoever between 'the pot does not exist here,' 'this [location] does not possess a pot,' and '[this is] other than [a location] with a pot.' Therefore, the seeing of the bare location as other than a pot-possessing location is itself the seeing of the absence of a pot. The cognition 'the pot does not exist here' is merely a <s>smṛti</s> (memory), having the nature of recognizing what has [already] been grasped. How is this known? Because immediately after perception, without any intervening process of establishing <s>anvaya</s> and <s>vyatireka</s>, one determines through the two subsequent conceptual cognitions: 'this is an entity of a location distinct from a pot' and 'this pot-entity does not exist [here].' Therefore, there is no tracing of <s>anvaya</s> and <s>vyatireka</s> here.

body.translated_text: Showing that the same parity applies to [the argument from] non-separate establishment (<s>apṛthaksiddhi</s>) as well, he says "upon the manifestation of the logical mark" (<s>liṅgāvirbhāve</s>) and so forth. This cognition directed at the object of another's existence, which is said to be a logical mark (<s>liṅga</s>) — of that [cognition], which has the form of a locus free from that [absence],

body.text: kiñca- dṛṣṭāntāsiddhe svātmanyabhāvaviṣayopalabdhistadabhāvasya sādhanaṃ | tadeva vyatirekamukhena darśayati- "tacca tasya" ityādi | ihāpyastyevānvaya iti cet, āha- "na hyevaṃ śakyam" ityādi | kasmānna śakya darśayitum? | tadekopalabdheḥ tasyaikasyānanyasaṃsargiṇo yopalabdhirviśeṣarūpā tasyāḥ kvacidapyanyatrābhāvāt | atha tadviviktopalabdhisāmānyaṃ heturūcyate- yatra yatra ghaṭaviviktabhūtalopalabdhistatra tatra ghaṭābhāvo yathā pūrvānubhūte ghaṭavivikte pradeśa ityāha- "sāmānyena pradarśane kriyamāṇe" dṛṣṭānte 'pi pūrvānubhūtaghaṭavivikte pradeśe ghaṭābhāvasya prasādhakaṃ pratyakṣādikaṃ pramāṇāntaramanyabhāvaviṣayopalabdhernāsti, kiṃ tu saiva tadanyabhāvopalabdhiḥ sādhyadharmasya tadabhāvalakṣaṇasya sādhikā | (

children.translated_text: <s>Hetubinduṭīkā</s> 202.

children.text: ) sā ca yathā sādhyadharmiṇi tadabhāvasiddhye dṛṣṭāntamapekṣate tathā dṛṣṭānte 'pi | tathā, tatrāpi tadanyatrāpītyanavasthā dṛṣṭāntānām iti | anavasthāyāṃ cāpratipattiḥ sarvatra tadabhāvasya | yata evaṃ "tasmānna" kutaścilliṅgāttadanyabhāvāttadupalabdhervā tadabhāvasiddhiriti | yadi tadanyabhāvastadabhāvaṃ na sādhayati, kiṃ punarlliṅgatayā sādhayati?, ityata āha- "so 'nyabhāvaḥ" pratyakṣalakṣaṇena- pratyakṣasyaiva vivakṣitopalambhādanyatvenānupalambhatvāt | tallakṣaṇenānupalambhena siddhaḥ sannabhāvavyavahāraṃ sādhayet, karmasthakriyāpekṣāyāṃ tadanyabhāvasyānupalabdhirūpatvāt | kva punarasāvabhāvavyavahāraṃ sādhayet? | mūḍhapratipattau sādhyāyāṃ | yastvamūḍho viṣayapratipattau viṣayiṇaṃ smaratyeva tasyābhāvavyavahāraḥ pratyakṣanibandhana eveti na tatrānupalabdherliṅgateti sucarccitamevānyatretīhālaṃ prasaṅgeneti |
children.translated_text: ) And just as that [apprehension] requires an example for establishing the absence of that in the property-locus to be proved, so too [it requires an example] in the example itself. And likewise, even there [it would require] yet another [example], and so on — resulting in an infinite regress of examples. And in the case of infinite regress, there would be non-cognition of the absence of that everywhere. Since this is so, "therefore not" — the establishment of the absence of that does not come about from any inferential mark, from the existence of another, or from the apprehension of that [other]. If the existence of another does not establish the absence of that, then what does it establish as an inferential mark? To this he says: "That existence of another" — by the definition of <s>pratyakṣa</s> (direct perception) — because it is non-apprehension by virtue of being other than perception itself, which is the intended apprehension. Being established through <s>anupalambha</s> (non-apprehension) characterized by that [perception], it would establish the conventional usage of absence, because the existence of another has the nature of non-apprehension when the action requires an agent. And where would it establish the conventional usage of absence? When the cognition of a confused person needs to be corrected. But for one who is unconfused, who in cognizing the object remembers the possessor of that object [as absent], the conventional usage of absence is grounded in <s>pratyakṣa</s> (direct perception) alone — so <s>anupalabdhi</s> (non-perception) is not an inferential mark in that case. This has been well discussed elsewhere, so enough with this digression.

body.translated_text: Moreover — when the example is unestablished, the apprehension of another entity that is devoid of the object of absence is the proof of that absence. He shows just this through the method of <s>vyatireka</s> (negative concomitance), saying: "And that, of that" and so forth. If [the opponent says:] here too there is indeed <s>anvaya</s> (positive concomitance), he responds: "For it cannot be shown thus" and so forth. Why can it not be shown? Because the apprehension of just that one — the apprehension of that single entity not conjoined with anything else — which is of a specific nature, is absent anywhere else. Now, if it is said that the general [fact of] apprehension of something distinct from that is stated as the reason — wherever there is apprehension of a ground-surface distinct from a pot, there is absence of a pot, as in a previously experienced location distinct from a pot — he says: "When a demonstration is being made in general terms," even in the example — in a previously experienced location distinct from a pot — there is no other <s>pramāṇa</s> such as <s>pratyakṣa</s> (direct perception) etc. that establishes the absence of a pot, apart from the apprehension of another entity as its object. Rather, that very apprehension of the existence of another is itself the establisher of the property to be proved, namely the absence of that. (

body.text: 3. anupalabdhiṃ tridhā vibhajya tadvivecanam |
body.translated_text: 3. Division of <s>anupalabdhi</s> (non-perception) into three kinds and their analysis.

body.text: tadevamanupalabdheraśeṣavipratipattinirākaraṇena svarūpamavasthāpyaprabhedanirddeśārthamāha- "seyaṃ yathoktā tridhānupalabdhiḥ" | katham? | siddhe tatprasādhakena pramāṇena kāryakāraṇabhāve sati kāraṇasyānupalabdhiḥ | kīdṛśasya? | siddhābhāvasya | tathā, vyāpyavyāpakabhāvasiddhau satyāṃ tatprasādhanapramāṇabalenaiva siddhābhāvasyaiva vyāpakasya nānyasya vyāpakānupalabdherevāsiddhatāprasaṅgād | yathoktā svabhāvānupalabdhiśceti | evaṃ trividhānupalabdhiḥ | kathaṃ punaḥ kāraṇavyāpakayorabhāvavyavahāraḥ sidhyati yatastayoḥ siddhābhāvatocyata ityāha- "tatra kāraṇavyāpakayorapi" na kevalaṃ yasya sākṣādabhāvavyavahāraḥ sādhyate | svabhāvānupalabdhau "svabhāvasyāsavdhyavahārasya siddhiranyasya" tadviviktasya bhāvasiddhiryā saivāsavdyavahārasiddhihetutvādevamucyate | "sa" kāraṇavyāpakābhāvaḥ "tathāsiddho" 'nyabhāvasiddhyā pratyakṣarūpayā siddho 'bhāvavyavahāraḥ kāryavyāpyayoḥ pratiṣedhyayoḥ | yadānayorvirūpaviṣayatayā saviśeṣāṇāmupalabdhirna (

children.text: ) sidhyati "tadābhāvamabhāvavyavahāraṃ vā sādhayati" | samuccayārtho vāśabdaḥ | atha kiṃ svabhāvānupalabdhāvapyabhāvo liṅgatayā sādhyata ityāha- "svabhāvānupalabdhau tu" ityādi | "abhāvavyavahāra eva", nābhāvo 'pi tasya pratyakṣasiddhatvāt |
children.translated_text: ) established, due to these [cause and pervader] having objects of different forms, "then it establishes the absence, or the conventional usage of absence." The word 'or' has the sense of conjunction. Now, is absence also established as an inferential mark in <s>svabhāvānupalabdhi</s> (non-apprehension of intrinsic nature)? He says: "But in <s>svabhāvānupalabdhi</s>" and so forth. "Only the conventional usage of absence" — not absence itself, because that is established by <s>pratyakṣa</s> (direct perception).

body.translated_text: Having thus established the essential nature of <s>anupalabdhi</s> (non-perception) by refuting all disagreements, he states the purpose of indicating its varieties: "This aforesaid <s>anupalabdhi</s> is threefold." How? Non-apprehension of the cause, when the causal relation has been established by a <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid cognition) that proves it. Of what kind? Of that whose absence is established. Likewise, when the relation of pervader and pervaded has been established, by the very force of the <s>pramāṇa</s> that proves it — only of the pervader whose absence is established, not of anything else, since otherwise there would be the unwanted consequence of the non-apprehension of the pervader being unestablished. And the non-apprehension of the intrinsic nature as described — thus <s>anupalabdhi</s> is threefold. But how is the conventional usage of absence established for cause and pervader, such that the absence of those two is spoken of? He says: "Regarding the cause and pervader too" — not only that whose conventional usage of absence is directly proved. In <s>svabhāvānupalabdhi</s> (non-apprehension of intrinsic nature), "the establishment of the intrinsic nature's conventional usage of absence is the establishment of the existence of another" — that which is distinct from it — and that very [establishment of the existence of another] is called thus because it is the cause of the establishment of the conventional usage of absence. "That" — the absence of cause and pervader — "established in that way" — established through the establishment of the existence of another, which is of the nature of <s>pratyakṣa</s> (direct perception) — is the conventional usage of absence with respect to effect and pervaded, which are the things to be negated. When the apprehension of specific instances is not (

body.text: atra parasya vacanāvakāśamāśaṅkayāha- "yadi" tarhi "kāraṇavyāpakau" siddho 'savdyavahāro yayoḥ tau santau | kena? | "tadanyasya" kāraṇavyāpakaviviktasya bhāvasya siddhiryā pratyakṣatmikā tadrūpayānupalabdhyā, anyasya kāryasya vyāpyasya vābhāvamabhāvavyavahāraṃ ca sādhayataḥ | sā cānyabhāvopalabdhistayoḥ kāraṇavyāpakayorupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptāveva satyāmasavdyavahārasya sādhikā nānyathā ityevamiṣyamāṇe sati kathaṃ tayoḥ kāraṇavyāpakānupalabdhyoḥ parokṣe 'rthe viṣaye prayogaḥ | yadā kāryasvabhāvahetvorvyatirekaprayogaḥ kriyate- yatra yatrāgnirnāsti tatra tatra dhūmo 'pi nāsti, tathā yatra yatra vṛkṣo nāsti kṣaṇikatā vā tatra tatra śiṃśapā nāsti sattvaṃ vā ityaśeṣapadārthaparigraheṇa vyatirekaprayoge sati | nahi tadāgnivṛkṣavyatiriktāḥ sarve 'rthāḥ pratyakṣatā(kṣā) akṣaṇikatā vā | tataśca kathaṃ tadviviktopalabdhilakṣaṇānupalabdhiḥ pratiyogino vopalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptatā siddhā? | tathā ca kathamaśeṣopasaṃhāreṇa vyāptyā kāryasvabhāvahetvo 'rvyatirekaḥ sidhyet? | tadasiddhau vā kathamanayorgamakatvam? | tasmāt kvacidadarśanamātrādeva vyatireka eṣṭavyaḥ, kvacicca darśanamātrādanvayaḥ | tathā ca pratibandhaghoṣaṇānarthiketi manyate paraḥ |
body.translated_text: Here, anticipating an occasion for the opponent's objection, he says: "If" then "the cause and pervader" — those two being such that the conventional usage of absence is established [for them]. By what? By the establishment of the existence of something distinct from the cause and pervader — which is of the nature of <s>pratyakṣa</s> (direct perception) — that is, by the non-apprehension [so characterized]; they establish the absence and the conventional usage of absence of another thing, namely the effect or the pervaded. And that apprehension of the existence of another establishes the conventional usage of absence for those two — the cause and the pervader — only when the apprehension-condition is fulfilled, not otherwise. If this is accepted, then how can there be application of these two — the non-apprehension of cause and the non-apprehension of pervader — to an object that is beyond perception? When the <s>vyatireka</s> (negative concomitance) of <s>kāryahetu</s> (effect-as-reason) and <s>svabhāvahetu</s> (nature-as-reason) is demonstrated: 'wherever fire does not exist, there smoke also does not exist'; and likewise, 'wherever a tree does not exist or momentariness does not exist, there a <s>śiṃśapā</s> tree does not exist, or existence does not exist' — when the <s>vyatireka</s> is demonstrated with an exhaustive inclusion of all objects. For at that time, not all objects that are other than fire or tree are perceptible, nor [are they all] non-momentary. And so, how is the non-apprehension characterized by the apprehension of what is distinct from that [established], or how is the apprehension-condition of the counter-positive established? And thus, how could the <s>vyatireka</s> of <s>kāryahetu</s> and <s>svabhāvahetu</s> be established through exhaustive <s>vyāpti</s> (pervasion)? Or if that is not established, how can these two be probative? Therefore, <s>vyatireka</s> should be accepted merely from non-observation in some cases, and <s>anvaya</s> merely from observation in some cases. And thus the proclamation of necessary connection is pointless — so the opponent thinks.

children.text: ) pūrvoktena pramāṇena vyāpyavyāpakabhāvasādhakena ca tadutpattilakṣaṇe tādātmyalakṣaṇe ca sambandhe sādhite siddhasambandhayoryadyabhāvo yatra yatrā bhāvaḥ syāt parasyāpi kāryasya vyāpyasya vāvaśyaṃ niyamenābhāvo 'nyathāhetukatvaprasaṅgāt, niḥsvabhāvatāprasaṅgācca | taddvāreṇa pratibandhaprasādhake pramāṇe smṛtiḥ kathaṃ nāma syādityetasyārthasya darśanārthamete kāraṇavyāpakānupalabdhī prayujyete iti | darśanādarśanabalena tu sādhane yatraivaikadarśane paro dṛṣṭo 'darśane vā na dṛṣṭaḥ tatraiva tasya bhāvo 'bhāvo vā bhavatu sarvatra tu kasmād bhavati? | na hyapratibaddhātmanāṃ gavāśvādīnāṃ kvacit tathābhāvadarśane 'pi sarvatra tathābhāvo bhavati, puruṣasya tu sarvadā kvacidekabhāvābhāvayoraparasya bhāvābhāvādarśanaṃ yadṛcchāsaṃvādaḥ sambhāvyeta asati pratibandhe | tathā cāha-
children.translated_text: ) as stated earlier, and by the <s>pramāṇa</s> that establishes the relation of pervader and pervaded — when the relation characterized by origination [from a cause] and the relation characterized by identity [of nature] have been established — if there is absence wherever there is absence of these [cause or pervader] whose relation is established, then necessarily, by rule, there is absence of the other thing too — the effect or the pervaded — otherwise there would be the unwanted consequence of it being caused by something else, and the unwanted consequence of lacking intrinsic nature. Through that [established connection], the non-apprehension of cause and pervader are applied for the purpose of demonstrating this meaning: how could there not be a <s>smṛti</s> (recollection) regarding the <s>pramāṇa</s> that establishes the necessary connection? But as for establishing [something] by the force of observation and non-observation alone — wherever one has observed one thing or not observed it — let the existence or absence of the other be [established] only there; why should it hold everywhere? For regarding cows, horses, and other things that do not have a necessary connection, even though one observes a certain state of affairs somewhere, that state of affairs does not hold everywhere. And for a person, the observation of the existence or absence of one thing always [conjoined with] the existence or absence of another somewhere could be suspected to be a chance coincidence in the absence of a necessary connection. And thus he says —

body.translated_text: The proponent says: "Not at all" — "the application" of the non-apprehension of cause and pervader to an object beyond perception at the time of demonstrating <s>vyatireka</s> "as a <s>pramāṇa</s>" — the non-apprehension of the cause or the pervader is never applied as a valid means of cognition. Why? "Because of the non-ascertainment of the inferential mark" — because the non-apprehension of cause and pervader, which is the nature of the inferential mark, or the absence of that, is of a doubtful nature — the absence of that being itself doubtful. How then is the application of these two accepted at that time? He says: "Merely" and so forth. For regarding the cause and pervader, by the <s>pramāṇa</s> that establishes the causal relation (
